## Perseverance Update: The Ghostly Rocks of ‘Idubi’ — Bright Remnants of Aqueous Systems from Long Ago

NASA’s Perseverance rover captured this image of a bright, silica-rich rock in the “Idubi” area using its left Mastcam-Z camera on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023) at the local mean solar time of 13:03:53.

NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU

Written by Candice Bedford, Research Scientist at Purdue University

Date: Nov. 16, 2026

During the Perseverance rover’s investigation of “Idubi” — an area of ancient Martian crust exposed in the “Lac de Charmes” region, outside of Jezero crater — the Perseverance rover team has been captivated by a cluster of eerily bright, light-toned rocks in the area. These bright fragments stand out sharply against the underlying darker and often dust-covered Martian surface, and are even brighter than the[igneous and impactite rocks we previously investigated.](https://science.nasa.gov/blog/mars-has-its-charmes/)Suspecting that they differed from the typical igneous rocks in the area, the rover team directed Perseverance to investigate. Newly downlinked data from the SuperCam instrument has confirmed that these light-toned rocks are not igneous in origin and instead are rich in hydrated silica.

Hydrated silica can form in many aqueous environments on the Earth, including hydrothermal, pedogenic, and groundwater systems. As such, these types of deposits are prime targets for understanding Mars’ hydrological history, as several of these environments could have been capable of supporting life. Furthermore, hydrated silica holds immense astrobiological value due to its remarkable capacity to preserve microfossils. Could these pale remnants of an ancient Martian water system hold signs of ancient life?

When Perseverance previously encountered [silica-rich rocks on the inner rim](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0012821X2500055X) of Jezero Crater, the deposits were too small to deploy proximity science instruments and gather the high-resolution chemical and mineralogical data needed to constrain their origin and biosignature preservation potential. Fortunately, the rocks at “Idubi” offer a much more promising scale, and a detailed proximity science campaign is already underway.

A close-up image of a silica-rich rock in the “Idubi” area using the Perseverance rover’s SHERLOC WATSON camera, located on the turret at the end of the rover’s robotic arm. This image was acquired on Oct. 29, 2026 (Sol 2023) at the local mean solar time of 17:33:55.

NASA/JPL-Caltech

articleBody:
Within the sprawling grounds of Mantua's Ducal Palace lies Piazza Pallone (now officially Piazza Lega Lombarda), a quiet, tree-lined square, few tourists notice the simple stone plaque mounted on the perimeter wall enclosing the space.

The plaque commemorates one of the darkest episodes of Mantuan Renaissance history: the beheading of Agnese Visconti on February 7, 1391.

Agnese, daughter of the Lord of Milan, Bernabò Visconti, was married at just fourteen years old to Francesco I Gonzaga, Lord of Mantua. Twelve years later, her husband accused her of adultery with the knight Antonio da Scandiano (also known as Vincenzo da Scalona). Her alleged lover was hanged in the square, while Agnese was beheaded at the age of 28 in the very same spot.

Historians generally agree that the accusation was a political setup orchestrated by Francesco I Gonzaga to sever ties with the Visconti family and forge a new alliance with the Republic of Venice. The bodies of both executed lovers were buried without ceremony in unconsecrated ground within the square.

Over the centuries, the injustice suffered by Agnese seemed to permeate the stones of the square, giving rise to one of Lombardy's most famous ghost stories.

It is said that on cold winter nights—particularly around the anniversary of her death in February—when dense fog from the Mincio River rolls over the palace courtyards, the shadowy figure of Agnese reappears near the plaque.

Local lore claims her headless spirit wanders desperately around the perimeter of the square searching for her severed head or clutching a stained shroud to her chest. Over the years, passersby have reported hearing heavy footsteps on the ground, the rustle of period garments, and a quiet weeping that cuts off abruptly right in front of the stone tablet.

Funnyly the XIX century plaque lists an incorrect age for the noblewoman at the time of her execution—a historical error preserved on the marble during restorations.

title: Kult um Jensen Huang: Ist Nvidia eher Sekte als Religion?

articleBody:
# Kult um Jensen Huang: Ist Nvidia eher Sekte als Religion?

(Bild: glen photo / Shutterstock.com )

Mehr als 180.000 Menschen fordern Huangs Rückkehr an die Nvidia-Spitze, Musk und Trump zeigen Sympathie. Das Problem dahinter ist älter als die Affäre.

Jensen Huang ist wie ein Popstar unter den führenden Tech-Managern. Das wird besonders jetzt deutlich, wenige Tage nach seinem Rücktritt. Inzwischen unterschrieben mehr als 180.000 Menschen eine Petition, die ihn wieder an der Spitze von Nvidia sehen will.

Die Initiative trägt den Namen "Stand With Jensen". Ihre Initiatoren fordern in einem offenen Brief, Huangs Rückkehr. Den Sachverhalt müssten Experten noch unabhängig klären.

Prominente Namen stehen in der Liste: Tesla-Chef Elon Musk unterzeichnete, ebenso Epic-Games-Chef Tim Sweeney. US-Präsident Donald Trump erklärte, er hätte nichts dagegen, wenn Huang wieder als CEO eingesetzt würde. Schließlich habe er "eine wichtige Lektion gelernt". Ob es Trump dabei wirklich um Huang geht oder um sein Vermögen, ist unklar. Laut Washington Post hielt Trump Ende August noch Nvidia-Aktien im Wert von bis zu 62 Millionen Dollar.

Das Board von Nvidia denkt bislang aber nicht daran, Huang zurückzuholen. So sagte es "eine mit der Sache vertraute Person" gegenüber Reuters. Jetzt zeigt die Kampagne, wovon sich das Board lösen muss: von einem Konzern, den Huang 33 Jahre lang um sich selbst errichtete.

### Wer unterschreibt

Von denen, die die Petition unterschrieben, gaben 8.800 an, selbst bei Nvidia zu arbeiten. Mehr als 94.000 bezeichneten sich selbst als Aktionäre – das kann sein, aber auch nicht, denn niemand prüfte das. Eine Umfrage der anonymen Berufsplattform Blind weist in dieselbe Richtung: Von den Nvidia-Mitarbeitern, die teilnahmen, wünschten sich 88 Prozent, dass Huang bleibt.

Der Rückhalt, den Huang in der Belegschaft genießt, zeigt sich auch in der internen Kommunikation. Das Magazin Wired zitiert eine Debatte in einer internen "Vorschlagsbox". Ein langjähriger Ingenieur forderte dort das Board auf, die Stimmung der Mitarbeiter zu berücksichtigen, bevor es Maßnahmen ergreift. In der Zwischenzeit kommt der Beitrag demnach auf mehr als 1.600 Kommentare.

Ein Kommentator schrieb laut Wired : "Wenn ihr an die Mission glaubt, holt DEN Chef zurück". Ein anderer meinte, Huang habe so viel Gutes getan, dass ihm eine zweite Chance zustehe. Schließlich sei er auch nur ein Mensch und könne Fehler machen.

### Vater des Volkes

In Taiwan, Huangs Geburtsland, gehen die Menschen noch weiter. Am Montag leuchtete am Wolkenkratzer Taipei 101 die Botschaft: "Taiwan Loves Jensen".

Lokale Medien betitelten ihn sogar als "Vater des Volkes", schrieb Reuters schon im Februar . Damals saß Huang bei einem Abendessen mit seinen wichtigsten Zulieferern. Seine Fans waren auch da. Laut Reuters verließ er das Essen immer wieder, begrüßte die Fans und gab Autogramme.

Ein Taiwaner zog jetzt gegenüber Reuters den Vergleich mit Steve Jobs. Den habe Apple einst auch hinausgedrängt, und er sei zurückgekehrt.

### Die Taylor Swift der Tech-Branche

Meta-Chef Mark Zuckerberg verglich Huang einmal mit Taylor Swift. Was die beiden verbindet, sagte er nicht. Lieder, inspiriert von gescheiterten Liebesbeziehungen, dürften es nicht sein. Vermutlich meinte Zuckerberg die Fähigkeit, Menschen in den Bann zu ziehen und in Massen zu Events strömen zu lassen.

Wie das aussieht, konnte Berlin im Oktober beobachten. Der Tagesspiegel berichtete davon . Die Menge strömte zu Huangs Rede auf der Nvidia-Konferenz GTC, und vor dem Tempodrom bildete sich eine Schlange, die einmal um einen Fußballplatz reichte. "Das hat für mich den Hype von ‘nem Taylor-Swift-Konzert", sagte ein Besucher demnach. Andere waren wegen der Inhalte bei der Konferenz und sagten der Zeitung, vom "Personenkult" um den Nvidia-Chef hielten sie nichts.

Ein Personenkult lässt sich auch zu Geld machen, wie im Juli eine Auktion zeigte. Sotheby's versteigerte eine von Huang signierte Lederjacke für 960.000 Dollar. Das Auktionshaus hatte sie vorab auf 40.000 bis 60.000 Dollar geschätzt. Beschrieben wurde das gute Stück als "Uniform eines ersten Gläubigen".

### Wer widerspricht

Niemand wird sich wundern, dass, wo Licht ist, auch Schatten ist. Biograf Stephen Witt beschrieb Huang in seinem Buch "The Thinking Machine" als Mensch voller Tatendrang und Charisma. Die dunkle Seite war, dass Huang voller Wut zu sein schien, wenn er sich von seinem Gegenüber missverstanden fühlte.

Im konkreten Fall ging es um ein Thema, das viele Menschen umtreibt: Vernichtet KI Arbeitsplätze? Huang störte sich anscheinend daran, dass diese Frage immer wieder aufkam. Witt schrieb: "Seine Wut schien ungezügelt, in alle Richtungen gerichtet und völlig unangemessen."

### Ein Konzern ohne Nummer zwei

Für ein Unternehmen mag es von Vorteil sein, wenn ein Visionär an der Spitze es antreibt und zu neuen Gipfeln führt. Was es aber bedeutet, wenn die Leitfigur fehlt, auf die Nvidia alles ausrichtete, beschreibt ein Kommentar bei Channel News Asia (CNA) .

Bis zu Huangs Rücktritt hatte Nvidia offenbar keinen Board-Vorsitzenden und auch keine Nummer zwei. Wer folgt auf Huang, wenn er ausfallen sollte? Einen Plan über seine Nachfolge veröffentlichte der Konzern nie. Und es gab kaum andere Manager, die ein großes Geschäftsfeld verantworteten, stattdessen kümmerten sie sich in erster Linie um einzelne Produkte und Techniken. Wenn Analysten Fragen hatten, antwortete Huang meist selbst.

Erst nach seinem Rücktritt ernannte das Board einen Vorsitzenden, wie Nvidia der Börsenaufsicht SEC mitteilte . Harvey C. Jones ist 73 Jahre alt und sitzt seit 1993 im Gremium. Laut Wired besteht das Board größtenteils aus frühen Investoren und langjährigen Vertrauten von Huang.

Der CNA -Kommentar zitiert den Harvard-Professor Rakesh Khurana, der einen Vergleich zu Sekten und Religionen zieht. Eine Religion unterscheide sich von einer Sekte dadurch, dass sie ihren Gründer überdauere. Nvidia, so die Autorin Beth Kowitt, gleiche eher der Sekte.

### Wie Apple und Amazon es lösten

Unersetzlich – das sagten Anhänger auch über Steve Jobs und Jeff Bezos. Irgendwann kamen beide Konzerne auch ohne ihre Gründer aus. Der Unterschied zu Nvidia ist aber, dass beide Gründer dies selbst vorbereiteten. Jobs baute Tim Cook als Nummer zwei auf und Cook vertrat ihn schon, als Jobs gegen seine Krankheit kämpfte. Bezos ließ Andy Jassy jahrelang das Cloudgeschäft führen, bevor er ihm den Chefposten übergab.

Bei Nvidia fehlt eine solche Figur. Der Telegraph zitierte Huang mit den Worten, er hoffe, der nächste Chef arbeite schon im Unternehmen. Wer das sein könnte, sagte er nicht. Ob er das nur so dahinsagte, weiß niemand genau. Umso sicherer sind sich seine Fans: Niemand könne Huang ersetzen. Der Investor Shaun Maguire von Sequoia schrieb auf X, Jensen sei für Amerikas Führung bei KI unersetzlich. Musk stimmte ihm zu.

### Wie das Board kontrollierte

Die besondere Position, die Huang im Konzern innehatte, zeigte sich auch im Verlauf der Affäre. Offenbar kontrollierte das Board ihn nicht ausreichend. Schon im Oktober täuschte er laut Reuters seinen Chefjuristen über die Beziehung zu Alice Huang. Als die Affäre aufflog, konnten Board-Mitglieder noch argumentieren, Huang sei in eine Honigfalle getappt. Am 8. November sprachen sie ihm noch das Vertrauen aus .

Zum Bruch kam es erst, nachdem die New York Times über eine Liaison mit einer ihm unterstellten Managerin berichtete. Das war ein klarer Verstoß gegen den Verhaltenskodex bei Nvidia, den die Board-Mitglieder nicht mehr deckten. Am 11. November nahmen sie seinen Rücktritt an.

Die Frage, ob Alice Huang eine chinesische Spionin ist, ist noch offen. Telepolis berichtete bereits , dass es dazu bislang keine belastbaren Erkenntnisse gibt. Laut Reuters versuchen die US-Geheimdienste noch immer herauszufinden, welche Informationen sie womöglich an Peking durchreichte.

### Ein Außenstehender?

Der Kampf um die Nachfolge ist inzwischen entbrannt. US-Finanzminister Scott Bessent fordert, dass Nvidia einen Außenstehenden an die Spitze holt. Der Konzern müsse sich "drastisch" umbauen. Prominente Investoren wie Brad Gerstner von Altimeter mahnen hingegen, das Board solle die Nachfolge nicht übereilen.

Der Technologieanalyst Richard Windsor erwartet, dass große institutionelle Anleger eine Rückkehr ablehnen, solange die Ermittler nicht fertig sind. Langfristig würden die Aktionäre aber von Huang profitieren, glaubt er. Kaum jemand kenne die Kunden und Zulieferer so gut, allen voran den Chipfertiger TSMC.

Am Dienstag legt Nvidia seine Quartalszahlen vor, die Telefonkonferenz beginnt um 23 Uhr deutscher Zeit. Zum ersten Mal, seit Huang Nvidia gründete, wird nicht er die Zahlen erklären, sondern Interimschefin Colette Kress. Die Aktie verlor am Montag 3,7 Prozent.

title: EFF’s AI Cybersecurity Policy Framework
subtitle: The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites.

articleBody:
The news has been filled with stories recently of AI breaching the security of websites. And while it may feel like a new problem because of AI’s involvement, it turns out that there are longstanding existing cybersecurity safety best practices that these companies—some of the largest tech companies in the world—could and should have taken to prevent these breaches.

Recent cybersecurity incidents have shown that some of the world’s largest tech companies have failed to take basic security precautions when testing frontier AI systems on internet-connected systems. Unfortunately, these failures resulted in breaches of numerous third-party websites, including an AI research-sharing platform called Hugging Face and the Australian healthcare system’s website. Even worse, AI developers failed to detect most of the incidents until long after they occurred due to inadequate monitoring of the AI systems during testing. Had the companies abided by basic, common sense security protocols, these incidents likely would not have occurred.

While the White House and leaders of major AI companies have claimed that no action is necessary, understandably, lawmakers at all levels and of both parties are proposing legislation to create new, additional safety protocols. These incidents may warrant legislative action. However, the good news is that post-incident reports indicate new protocols are largely unnecessary. Following existing best practices would have been enough to prevent the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident and others like it. In other words, responsible AI developers can take immediate action to protect the public by implementing well-established security precautions as they develop and test their systems.

Lawmakers should start by referencing existing legal protections, including claims like negligence, gross negligence, trespass to chattels, Section 1201 of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA), and computer trespass statutes like the Consumer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) and analogous state law provisions, such as Section 502 of the California Penal Code.

Policymakers can help protect the public by requiring AI developers to follow established security protocols—and creating legal liability for failing to do so. These policies would protect the public from irresponsible actions by AI developers without impeding innovation. To the extent that gaps in existing laws warrant new legislation, EFF recommends the following policy framework:

STATUTORY SECURITY REQUIREMENTS: Lawmakers should enact legislation that requires AI developers to adhere to well-established cybersecurity best practices when testing AI systems, such as strong sandboxing and network isolation, least-privilege access, effective logging and monitoring, and clear incident-response procedures

REGULATORY STANDARDS: Congress should require an existing federal agency, such as the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)1, to adopt safety standards for pre-deployment development and testing of generative AI systems, based on the established best practices referenced above. The agency should be required to update the standards every 2 years, or earlier as needed due to reported security incidents and/or major technological advancements. These standards should be developed in consultation with academic and nonprofit AI researchers, civil liberties organizations, and commercial AI developers, and adopted through formal agency rulemaking following a notice and comment process. That consultation should include an assessment of potential adverse impacts on competition, with the goal of ensuring that regulatory standards do not effectively lock out potential competitors.

LIABILITY: The law should provide for civil liability for AI development and testing that results in unauthorized access to a third party system, if performed under conditions that do not satisfy cybersecurity standards adopted by NIST, or another federal agency responsible for adopting these regulations, unless the company proves it acted reasonably under the circumstances to prevent unauthorized access to third party system

ENFORCEMENT: Both federal and state authorities should be able to hold AI developers accountable where they have failed to meet the minimum standards adopted by the designated federal agency, such as NIST. Providing for state—in addition to federal—enforcement power reduces the risk of regulatory capture. Regulators should require independent investigations and notification of affected parties in the event of a security incident involving unauthorized access to a third party’s computer system. Finally, legislation should include an appropriately targeted private right of action.

The public shouldn’t have to worry about the risks of reckless AI development—or give up the benefits of AI just to prevent irresponsible developers from causing harm. By adopting policies that address demonstrated risks, lawmakers can provide meaningful public protection without hampering the development of useful tools.

1NIST, the NSA, and CISA have recently issued a set of voluntary practices for managing security incidents during the training and evaluation of AI agents. Those practices may inform but do not substitute for the regulatory standards that should be developed according to the public, participatory process outlined here.

articleBody:
A humanoid robotics company backed and advised by President Donald Trump’s son, Eric Trump, has reportedly missed payroll and may be on the brink of collapse after a funding shortfall. The Silicon Valley startup, Foundation Future Industries, claims it is developing and testing robots for military roles on battlefields from Ukraine to Gaza.

Foundation failed to pay employees for the payroll period ending on October 30, [anonymous sources told CNBC](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/14/foundation-payroll-ceo-loan.html). The startup’s staff is especially angry because Foundation’s co-founder and CEO, [Sankaet Pathak](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sankaet), supposedly borrowed $4.6 million in company funds to buy a luxury home overlooking San Francisco Bay about a year ago.

This comes as Pathak and Foundation’s leadership are still looking to raise funding to support a $3 billion valuation, based on their promise to develop a humanoid robot ready for combat duty and capable of wielding various weapons.

## Kidnapped Teen Rescued After Using ‘Among Us’ Video Game Chat to Secretly Ask Another Player for Help

[↗ Primärquelle: mymodernmet.com](https://mymodernmet.com/teenager-rescued-using-among-us/)

[Video games](https://mymodernmet.com/worlds-largest-game-tetris/) get a bad rap. Though they’re often looked down upon as a distracting outlet for young adults, despite the creativity and problem-solving that’s often involved, it turns out they can also be essential in saving lives. Teenager Kylie Arellano was rescued after allegedly being held captive for more than 500 days, thanks to an unlikely connection she made with another player through the popular online game [Among Us](https://www.innersloth.com/games/among-us/).

An online multiplayer game that uses social deduction to seek out the “impostors” in a group of players, *Among Us* rose in popularity during the COVID-19 pandemic and served as a great way for friends to keep in touch during quarantine. For Arellano, who went missing from her Utah home in May 2025, the game’s ability to connect players with one another ultimately became a crucial part of her rescue.

Arellano was allegedly held captive in the basement of 39-year-old Adam Hunter Harmel’s home in Huntington, Oregon. Although Harmel had reportedly taken away her original phone, he eventually gave her another device that could connect to Wi-Fi but had no cellular service. This allowed Arellano to play *Among Us* and, more importantly, communicate with other people through the game.

In mid-October 2026, Arellano began talking with another player she met while playing *Among Us*. Their conversations eventually moved to another social media platform, where she revealed her identity and explained that she was being held against her will. The other player (a child) told their mother, who contacted the FBI.

On November 1, the FBI monitored a video call between Arellano and the other player’s family, during which she shared details about her situation. Authorities were able to rescue her from the Oregon home that same day. Harmel was subsequently charged with transporting a minor across state lines with the intent to engage in criminal sexual activity.

While *Among Us* was originally designed as a way for players to work together and identify hidden impostors, for Arellano, it became something much more important. The game provided her with a way to reach the outside world, ultimately helping bring her captivity to an end.

title: Sorry, Robert Pattinson Is Not James Bond

articleBody:
Robert Pattinson is, I’m sure, a fine actor. I cannot vouch for this because I have not seen him in movies I’ve liked. Granted, I have not seen his entire body of work; I was already in my 40s when he landed his big role as a vampire in *Twilight*, a movie that was not exactly aimed at my demographic. I am a fan of superhero movies, and he was, in my view, a terrible Batman: He made Bruce Wayne into a dull cop in a costume. Still, he seems to be working a lot, so someone out there likes him.

But is he James Bond? No. Amazon MGM Studios, which now owns the movie franchise, announced today that he’ll take over the role. Yet Pattinson lacks the manly gravitas, the physicality, the wit, to play the world’s most dangerous spy.

I’m a Bond superfan. As a kid, I saw the Sean Connery movies only on television. I was 13 when I saw my first Bond film on a big screen: *Live and Let Die*, starring Roger Moore. It was a revelation. (I was old enough to start getting the jokes about sex, for one thing.) I then devoured, in proper sequence, all the Ian Fleming novels that inspired the movies. When I visited London as a teen in 1975, I didn’t care about seeing Parliament or the crown jewels. I wanted to be Moore—hey, he was the only movie Bond working at the time—and wander the streets once walked by the British spy who always saved the world and got the girl.

I know the voice, mannerisms, and quips of every cinematic Bond. I also know what Fleming’s Bond looks and sounds like. According to Fleming, he was based on the 1940s bandleader Hoagy Carmichael, if that makes any sense to you, and I even know where Bond’s boss, M, has his office and his favorite club. (I also know his full name: Miles Messervy. You’re welcome.) I know what Bond’s maid, May, makes him every day for breakfast.

In other words, I know James Bond. James Bond is a friend of mine. And Robert Pattinson, you are no James Bond.

*[[From the March 2024 issue: The James Bond trap](https://www.theatlantic.com/magazine/archive/2024/03/ian-fleming-killing-james-bond/677175/?utm_source=feed)]*

Bond does not need to be a hairy bruiser; in the movies he loses plenty of fights, and in the books he routinely gets beaten to a pulp and ends up in the enemy’s clutches. Connery was perhaps the most macho of the Bonds, whereas Moore was the most dainty. All of them, however, were charismatic rogues, mature adults who could shoot, fight, drink, and—well, other things. They enjoyed every martini and they made a play for every shapely woman who crossed their path. (Bond is suave and a hero, but he’s also a boozy, sexist boor.)

Can Pattinson carry the legacy of any of his predecessors? Aficionados will disagree on who made the best Bond, but each actor had a niche. Connery was a product of the Cold War and the swinging ’60s. (He came back to play Bond once in 1971, *Diamonds Are Forever*, a misfire that included fitting him with a bad toupee; he made one more mediocre Bond film in 1983 with a different production company as a one-off outside the “canonical” Bond series.) A temporary replacement Bond, an Australian named George Lazenby, did a fine job in one movie, and then blew his career by walking away from the character. Moore, like the rest of us, did his best to make his way through the silly 1970s, but I think he is underappreciated: His 007 grimly faced down Christopher Lee in *The Man With the Golden Gun* and dispatched not one but two genocidal freaks bent on planetary destruction: a web-fingered weirdo in *The Spy Who Loved Me* and a eugenics-obsessed, space-industry billionaire—a plot clearly ahead of its time—in *Moonraker*.

Moore was a decent Bond, but stayed with the role too long. In 1985, the 57-year-old Moore had a love scene with 36-year-old Grace Jones in *A View to a Kill*. Let us not speak of it again.

Timothy Dalton, another underappreciated Bond, was an accomplished Shakespearean actor who moved into the role easily, and brought a combination of Connery’s violent physicality and Moore’s caddish humor. (Watch the pre-credits sequence of *The Living Daylights*, which is one of the best cold opens in the entire series.) Producers had begun looking at the next Bond, Pierce Brosnan, when he was still playing the TV detective Remington Steele and was too young and callow to play a spy who was licensed to kill. But as he matured, he was an obvious choice to play Bond perhaps like no actor since Connery. Brosnan took Bond into the new, post–Cold War world with style, but also with murderous determination: In *GoldenEye*, one of the best Bond movies, Brosnan looks directly into his best friend’s face and then drops him to his death.

All of these men as Bond exuded a kind of energetic and masculine combination of professionalism and uncontrollable individuality. In the books, 007 is a complex character who soldiers on because it’s his job. He is sometimes morose and regretful. But all of that anguish would make for a drab series of movies, and to their credit, Connery, Lazenby, Moore, Brosnan, and even the dour Dalton manage to look they’re having fun—at least when they’re not about to be cut in half by lasers or strangled by a python.

Here I will aggravate a lot of Bond fans: I think the series went off the rails with the casting of Daniel Craig and a drastic change in the 007 scripts. Instead of taking on supervillains, Bond tussled with terrorists and financiers, all while thinking and talking way too much about his psyche. Craig, another fine actor, was *too* brutish, and the scripts make plain that the job did, in fact, get to him. Craig’s Bond dressed well enough, but he always seemed uncomfortable in his suits: He’s a brawler with deep, complicated feelings, and one thing the cinematic James Bond does not need is a lot of *feelings*. The Craig scripts became like therapy sessions: When the big reveal came in the Craig movie *Spectre—* that the sadistic, megalomaniacal genius Ernst Blofeld was actually just a little boy with hurt feelings whose dad liked Jimmy Bond better when they were kids—I nearly walked out of the theater. (And by the way, what an utter waste of Christoph Waltz, who was *born* to play Blofeld.)

He’s a walking young-Millennial stereotype, is what I’m saying.

*[[Read: Leave James Bond alone](https://www.theatlantic.com/newsletters/archive/2022/01/leave-james-bond-alone/676416/?utm_source=feed)]*

He doesn’t appear old or tough or coldly professional enough to be Bond. Think of this: Connery was 31 when he filmed *Dr. No* and 32 in *From Russia With Love*. Moore was 44 in *Live and Let Die*. Dalton was 41 when he strapped on his Walther PPK. Craig was 37 when he sat at the card table in *Casino Royale*. Pattinson is 40—and yet all of these guys look self-assured and old enough to play Pattinson’s father, not his colleague. (Even Brosnan seems like a tougher old brother, not a fellow Double-O.)

Having most recently watched Pattinson mumble and anguish his way through *The Batman*, I cannot imagine him driving a Soviet tank through the streets of Russia, lecturing M on the finer points of blending cognac, or gently pushing the bad guy out of a space station’s airlock with an invitation to “take a giant step for mankind.” Perhaps the next film will do wonders; Moore, for one, was usually better when the scripts stuck to action instead of cheap comedy. But I have no faith, after the Craig psychodramas, that the writers will rescue Pattinson—or Bond.

Amazon MGM is trying hard to work up a new image for Pattinson. Their [first look](https://x.com/007/status/2122343950308540474?a=tGwxhUs1dQOSPhJXsnU&s=20) has him in a tux sighting a sniper rifle, his face half-shadowed and his hair (for once) combed. Maybe it’ll work. But I still cannot imagine him trading barbs with the likes of Goldfinger: I imagine that when the mad criminal offers him a mint julep, Pattinson will scowl and explain that alcohol and sugar are bad for you.

articleBody:
# Falcon 9 flies national security doubleheader

## Rocket launches this week

On Wednesday, Nov. 18 , China is expected to launch a Long March 2D from the Taiyuan Satellite Launch Center in Shanxi province at 5:50 p.m. EST, according to NextSpaceflight . The payload has not been announced.

Later that night on Wednesday, Nov. 18 , SpaceX will launch the classified USSF-317 mission for the U.S. Space Force from Space Launch Complex 4E (SLC-4E) at Vandenberg Space Force Base in California at 10:00 p.m. EST. Neither SpaceX nor the Space Force has said what the rocket carries. The Falcon 9 booster will land on the droneship Of Course I Still Love You in the Pacific Ocean.

On Friday, Nov. 20 , a Long March 8A is slated to lift off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on Hainan Island at 6:00 a.m. EST, per NextSpaceflight . The payload has not been disclosed, but is suspected to be a batch of SatNet low-Earth-orbit (LEO) satellites for Guowang — a state-backed broadband megaconstellation meant to rival Starlink.

Closing out the week on Saturday, Nov. 21 , the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) will launch NROL-136 on a Falcon 9 from SLC-4E at 7:30 a.m. EST. Rather than heading for a droneship, the booster will fly back to Landing Zone 4.

## Rocket launches last week

Last week opened on Wednesday, Nov. 11, at 6:41 a.m. EST, when a Long March 2D lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center carrying CAS Pathfinder-1. The Chinese Academy of Sciences built the satellite to test key technologies for its planned Origins space science program, CGTN reported . Later that night, at 11:36 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched the classified USSF-627 mission from Vandenberg after two postponements. The booster landed on Of Course I Still Love You .

On Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:47 p.m. EST, SpaceX launched Starship Flight 15 from Starbase, Texas, aiming to catch both stages with its launch tower for the first time. SpaceX was unable to catch the Super Heavy booster after its onboard guidance system made the call to abort the attempt. Instead it exploded over the Gulf of Mexico just before reaching the water. The ship, on the other hand, reached orbit, the second Starship ever to do so, and released 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

Then on Saturday afternoon, after 14 trips around Earth, the rocket’s upper stage slowed over Starbase, dropped between the tower’s mechanical “chopsticks,” and was plucked out of the air. The catch was a first for SpaceX and spaceflight in general — no other spacecraft has ever entered orbit and then been caught at its launch site.

Russia launched a mission from the Vostochny Cosmodrome at 8:16 p.m. EST on Friday, Nov. 13. The Soyuz-2.1b carried a pair of high-resolution imaging satellites and a dozen smaller payloads.

Rocket Lab marked a milestone just after midnight on Saturday, Nov. 14. At 12:30 a.m. EST, its Electron rocket flew for the 100th time on The Mountain God Rises , lifting off from Launch Complex 1 on New Zealand’s Māhia Peninsula. The rocket placed a synthetic aperture radar satellite into orbit for the Japanese company iQPS. Synthetic aperture radar bounces microwaves off the ground to build images, letting it see through clouds and darkness.

The week ended in a loss. On Sunday, Nov. 15, at 12:40 p.m. EST, United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station carrying 40 satellites for Amazon Leo , the company’s broadband constellation. It was Vulcan’s return to flight after the USSF-87 mission in February — which experienced a minor booster anomaly despite successfully delivering its payload — and the first of several dozen Vulcan launches Amazon has booked. About 10 minutes into the flight, ULA reported an anomaly, and the satellites never reached orbit.

> Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit. Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us… — ULA (@ulalaunch) November 15, 2026

## Upcoming rocket launches

On Monday, Nov. 23, Arianespace is targeting 5:12 a.m. EST to launch an Ariane 64 from the Guiana Space Centre in French Guiana with 36 more Amazon Leo satellites.

Later on Monday, Nov. 23, SpaceX is slated to launch the classified USSF-266 mission for the Space Force from Vandenberg at 11:04 a.m. EST.

On Tuesday, Nov. 24, China is slated to launch a Long March 12 from the commercial launch site at Wenchang on Hainan Island at 2:00 a.m. EST, according to Next Spaceflight . The payload has not been confirmed, but is likely another batch of SatNet LEO satellites for Guowang.

On Thursday, Nov. 26, a launch window opens for the third flight of Isar Aerospace’s Spectrum rocket from Andøya Spaceport in Norway, according to European Spaceflight . Its payloads include AT-Astra, an Austrian technology-demonstration satellite built by Vienna-based R-Space. Spectrum reached orbit for the first time on its second flight in September.

On Sunday, Nov. 29, NASA and Northrop Grumman are targeting 10:47 a.m. EST to launch the NG-25 Cygnus XL cargo spacecraft on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station. Named the S.S. James A. Lovell after the beloved Apollo 13 commander, the spacecraft will haul several tons of supplies to the space station.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy , based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

articleBody:
As an open source maintainer, I get a lot of AI slop PRs. Some of these have genuine value. Most address edge cases that almost never occur in real life. It's not that they're not fixing real problems, it's that they're fixing problems that nobody is ever likely to encounter.

I'm experimenting with "proof of use" as a requirement for submissions. Specifically, you need to show me that your project that depends on my project before I'll look at your PR.

"Proof of use" can be an existing open source project that imports mine (show me the git history!) or a clear description starting with "in our closed source project in production, we found that...".

The specific problem that I want to address is ensuring that contributions from people genuinely depending on my software are handled, while filtering out the OpenClaw/Github green square farming/drive-by LLM noise.

What are lobste.rs's thoughts on this?

articleBody:
Did King Charles III deliver an address that included the words "my son has"? No, that's not true: Neither the royal family website nor news reports said anything like this. The article carrying that headline later acknowledged in its body that there was no evidence of such an address.

The claim appeared in [an article](https://unitednews360.com/1-minute-ago-king-charles-iii-issues-an-urgent-address-to-the-entire-uk-amid-overwhelming-grief-his-voice-trembling-as-he-reveals-my-son-has/) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261116205250/https://unitednews360.com/1-minute-ago-king-charles-iii-issues-an-urgent-address-to-the-entire-uk-amid-overwhelming-grief-his-voice-trembling-as-he-reveals-my-son-has/) ) on the unitednews360 website published on Nov. 15, 2026, under the title:

> 1 MINUTE AGO: King Charles III issues an URGENT address to the entire UK amid overwhelming grief, his voice trembling as he reveals: 'My son has...

This is what the image looked like on the website at the time of writing:

*(Image source: Unitednews360.)*

However, there was no such address.

A search across the British royal family's official website showed [no speech containing the phrase "My son has"](https://www.royal.uk/media-centre/press-releases?mrf=3&text=%22My%20son%20has%22&dates%5Bmin%5D=2023-05-05&dates%5Bmax%5D=2026-11-16) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261116210530/https://www.royal.uk/media-centre/press-releases?mrf=3&text=%22My%20son%20has%22&dates%5Bmin%5D=2023-05-05&dates%5Bmax%5D=2026-11-16) ) delivered by King Charles III between his coronation on May 6, 2023, and this writing:

*(Image source: Royal.uk.)*

[A search](https://news.google.com/search?q=King%20Charles%20III%20son%20address&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) across Google News (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261116211258/https://news.google.com/search?q=King%20Charles%20III%20son%20address&hl=en-US&gl=US&ceid=US%3Aen) ) for the phrase "King Charles III son address" didn't reveal news coverage about the so-called announcement.

The article about the supposed speech said the following near the end:

>... there is currently no verified evidence that King Charles has delivered an emergency national address announcing a tragedy involving Prince Harry. The dramatic quotation circulating online should therefore be treated as unconfirmed.

The image of crying King Charles III was AI-generated, as [SynthID Detector](https://synthid.com/image-detection) (archived [↗ web.archive.org](https://web.archive.org/web/20261116212228/https://synthid.com/image-detection) ), [Hive Moderation](https://hivemoderation.com/ai-generated-content-detection) and[ZeroGPT](https://www.zerogpt.com/ai-image-detector) showed:

*(Image source: SynthID.)*

*(Image source: Hive Moderation.)*

*(Image source: ZeroGPT.)*

# Credit without debit: A new way for hackers to target bank accounts

November 16, 2026

## Credit without debit: A new way for hackers to target bank accounts

edited by Robert Egan

Robert Egan

Senior Editor

This article has been reviewed according to Science X's editorial process and policies . Editors have highlighted the following attributes while ensuring the content's credibility:

fact-checked

trusted source

proofread

Researchers at the University of Massachusetts Amherst have discovered how, during a bank-to-bank transfer, money can be deposited into one bank account without the funds ever leaving the second bank. This new class of cyberthreat is called credit without debit (CWD), and the researchers have demonstrated three ways hackers can use it to steal money.

"Our goal is to strengthen financial security," says Taqi Raza, assistant professor in the Riccio College of Engineering at UMass Amherst. "The way we strengthen it is we find the loopholes and tell the banks, 'Okay, fix this problem.'"

## The two-day settlement window

Unlike previous research by this group, which focused on credit card and digital wallet vulnerabilities, this new study examines debit transactions, or ACH transactions. This system permanently moves money between banks—as opposed to creating a debt—and enables any bank-to-bank transaction, including direct deposit of salaries, bill payments (including credit card bills), mortgage services and withdrawals from digital wallets and various payment apps.

The way an ACH transaction should work is that transfers are processed through multistage interbank clearing and settlement. Consider the situation where a person has bank accounts at two different banks and wants to move money from Bank A into Bank B. The person initiates the transfer from Bank B, which pulls the funds from the account at Bank A.

The transaction is authorized when Bank B recognizes that Bank A has a valid routing and account number and then authorizes the transaction. There is a two-day payment processing window for Bank A to transfer the money, so to expedite access to funds, some banks provisionally post funds in their customers' accounts (in this example, Bank B posts these funds). Bank A checks that its customer's account has sufficient funds, that there is valid authorization and that there are no account holds, and then sends the money to Bank B. The interbank settlement is complete.

## Frozen accounts expose a costly mismatch

However, in a CWD attack, the attacker finds a victim with a frozen account, meaning the account can receive money but not send it. They link the victim's account to their own and then pull the victim's funds into their own account. The attacker's bank posts the provisional funds. However, because the victim's account is frozen, the settlement payment is never made.

In the two days it takes for this payment to be processed and rejected, the attacker has withdrawn the provisional funds, resulting in a direct financial loss to the bank. The researchers have created an interactive graphic to demonstrate how this attack works.

"The key root cause of all these attacks is that banks have treated distinct security checkpoints as interchangeable," explains Raza.

Once they discovered the vulnerabilities, the researchers coordinated with affected banks to resolve the issues, which have not been reproducible since. The team presented their paper on the work at the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS), 2026 .

## Beyond bank-to-bank transfers

The researchers found two additional instances where this credit-without-debit logic resulted in successful attacks. One attack used microdeposits from third-party payment apps used to verify bank account ownership; the other paid off a credit card bill using a frozen account.

"We focused on what the user can observe and what they can influence from their banking apps," says Ali Malik, a doctoral candidate in electrical and computer science at UMass Amherst. "They can initiate payments, they can cancel those at random moments, they can observe the progress of that transaction as it moves from processing, to settle, to cancel, to rejected. It's simple stuff. We defined our threat model around that."

Even with these vulnerabilities discovered, Raza recommends that consumers always follow security best practices, such as enabling two-factor authentication, monitoring bank statements for fraudulent activity and turning on text, email or banking app notifications whenever a debit or credit happens on an account.

More information

Ali Hamza Malik et al., Credit Without Debit: Formal Verification of Banking Payment Systems, Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (2026). DOI: 10.1145/3830454.3846614 Provided by University of Massachusetts Amherst Who's behind this story? Robert Egan Bachelor's in mathematical biology, Master's in creative writing. Well-traveled with unique perspectives on science and language. Full profile →

## The two-day settlement window

Unlike previous research by this group, which focused on credit card and digital wallet vulnerabilities, this new study examines debit transactions, or ACH transactions. This system permanently moves money between banks—as opposed to creating a debt—and enables any bank-to-bank transaction, including direct deposit of salaries, bill payments (including credit card bills), mortgage services and withdrawals from digital wallets and various payment apps.

The way an ACH transaction should work is that transfers are processed through multistage interbank clearing and settlement. Consider the situation where a person has bank accounts at two different banks and wants to move money from Bank A into Bank B. The person initiates the transfer from Bank B, which pulls the funds from the account at Bank A.

The transaction is authorized when Bank B recognizes that Bank A has a valid routing and account number and then authorizes the transaction. There is a two-day payment processing window for Bank A to transfer the money, so to expedite access to funds, some banks provisionally post funds in their customers' accounts (in this example, Bank B posts these funds). Bank A checks that its customer's account has sufficient funds, that there is valid authorization and that there are no account holds, and then sends the money to Bank B. The interbank settlement is complete.

## Frozen accounts expose a costly mismatch

However, in a CWD attack, the attacker finds a victim with a frozen account, meaning the account can receive money but not send it. They link the victim's account to their own and then pull the victim's funds into their own account. The attacker's bank posts the provisional funds. However, because the victim's account is frozen, the settlement payment is never made.

In the two days it takes for this payment to be processed and rejected, the attacker has withdrawn the provisional funds, resulting in a direct financial loss to the bank. The researchers have created an interactive graphic to demonstrate how this attack works.

"The key root cause of all these attacks is that banks have treated distinct security checkpoints as interchangeable," explains Raza.

Once they discovered the vulnerabilities, the researchers coordinated with affected banks to resolve the issues, which have not been reproducible since. The team presented their paper on the work at the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security (CCS), 2026 .

## Beyond bank-to-bank transfers

The researchers found two additional instances where this credit-without-debit logic resulted in successful attacks. One attack used microdeposits from third-party payment apps used to verify bank account ownership; the other paid off a credit card bill using a frozen account.

"We focused on what the user can observe and what they can influence from their banking apps," says Ali Malik, a doctoral candidate in electrical and computer science at UMass Amherst. "They can initiate payments, they can cancel those at random moments, they can observe the progress of that transaction as it moves from processing, to settle, to cancel, to rejected. It's simple stuff. We defined our threat model around that."

Even with these vulnerabilities discovered, Raza recommends that consumers always follow security best practices, such as enabling two-factor authentication, monitoring bank statements for fraudulent activity and turning on text, email or banking app notifications whenever a debit or credit happens on an account.

More information

Ali Hamza Malik et al., Credit Without Debit: Formal Verification of Banking Payment Systems, Proceedings of the 2026 ACM SIGSAC Conference on Computer and Communications Security (2026). title: The Intercept Sues U.S. Military Over Iran Casualty Tally and Blacklist of Journalists
subtitle: The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon in a pair of lawsuits demanding the release of documents related to…
feedText: casualties in its war on Iran and the Department of Defense’s secretive blacklist of journalists. articleBody:
The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation sued Pete Hegseth’s Pentagon in a pair of lawsuits demanding the release of documents related to the number of U.S. casualties in its war on Iran and the Department of Defense’s secretive blacklist of journalists.

One [lawsuit](https://democracyforward.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/26-9964-Intercept-Iran-War-Complaint.pdf), filed on Friday, responds to the department’s “repeated, unexplained changes” to its publicly available tracker showing U.S. service members killed or injured in the conflict with Iran — including a [failure to acknowledge](https://theintercept.com/2026/10/12/iran-war-casualties-death-toll-accuracy/) one soldier’s death for the six months after he died — that were [documented](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/04/us-military-casualties-count-iran-war/) by Intercept reporter Nick Turse. The shifting figures led one defense official to call the undercount a “[casualty cover-up](https://theintercept.com/2026/04/01/iran-war-us-casualty-numbers-trump-hegseth/).”

In August, Turse requested from the Pentagon, through the Freedom of Information Act, casualty-related records and briefing materials presented to Defense Secretary Hegseth and his chief of staff, directives and guidance on casualties, as well as communications related to casualties between Hegseth and his staff of advisers. A later request filed by The Intercept in September sought the [financial costs](https://theintercept.com/2026/05/12/hegseth-pentagn-budget-defense-iran-war-cost/) of the [Iran war](https://theintercept.com/2026/10/01/trump-military-true-cost-budget-pentagon-trillions/) since its start in February. In all cases, the government stopped responding to The Intercept and has failed to provide any documents.

> “They need to come clean to the American people.”

A [second lawsuit](https://www.documentcloud.org/documents/28913341-fpf-intercept-media-v-dod-26-4041-compl/) against Hegseth’s DoD, filed on Monday, follows a July conversation with The Intercept in which a spokesperson for U.S. Central Command admitted the military post keeps [a blacklist of media members](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/24/pentagon-military-journalist-blacklist-press-media/). While reporting on the shifting U.S. soldier casualty figures, the CENTCOM spokesperson, Richard Allee, threatened Turse that he would be “put on a list of people to disregard” for calling the command too often.

[Related Pentagon Spokesperson Admits There’s a Secret Blacklist of Journalists](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/24/pentagon-military-journalist-blacklist-press-media/)

CENTCOM later denied the existence of such a list. But Turse spoke with an unnamed U.S. official who confirmed that “Hegseth’s office had a standing order not to engage with [Turse] and would deny it if challenged.” During the first Trump administration, Turse had been placed on a [separate blacklist](https://theintercept.com/2018/01/13/we-dont-consider-you-a-legitimate-journalist-how-i-got-blacklisted-by-the-pentagons-africa-command/.) kept by U.S. Africa Command, also within the Pentagon, after he reported on the torture of prisoners at a remote military base in Cameroon used by the U.S. for drone surveillance.

Turse has since filed a public records request seeking a copy of any “lists of journalists that CENTCOM discriminates against or disregards.” The Freedom of the Press Foundation also filed a request for communications and guidance related to the blacklist, as well as any records related to the command’s response to Turse’s article on the matter, [published in August](https://theintercept.com/2026/08/24/pentagon-military-journalist-blacklist-press-media/). The government has yet to provide any such information to The Intercept or Freedom of the Press Foundation.

“The military doesn’t get to decide which reporters it speaks to or ignores, especially when it’s engaged in legally questionable military actions and the human cost is at its highest. It’s not just the journalists who are harmed when the Pentagon behaves this way — the public and Congress are each denied critical information about what the military is doing in our name and with our taxes,” said Lauren Harper, Daniel Ellsberg chair on government secrecy, who filed FOIA requests for the blacklist on behalf of FPF. “If the Defense Department refuses to answer basic questions about how it engages with journalists, we’ll use the Freedom of Information Act to compel them in court.

The Intercept’s Turse called the Pentagon’s journalist blacklist “fundamentally un-American” and a way to avoid accounting for the real human toll of the ongoing war.

“Central Command wants to keep the sordid details of its wars — from civilian casualties in Iran and Yemen to U.S. military casualties across the Middle East — under wraps,” he said. “They need to come clean to the American people. We have to hold them accountable.”

[Related Next Time, Impeach Pete Hegseth for Press Censorship](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/13/pete-hegseth-impeachment-censorship-brendan-carr/)

Hegseth’s Department of Defense has long been hostile toward members of the media. In February 2025, days after Hegseth assumed office, the department forced out outlets such as NBC News, NPR, the New York Times, Politico, CNN, and the Washington Post from their Pentagon press desks. That October, Hegseth issued a new requirement in which journalists could only gain access to the Pentagon if they pledged to only report on information from government employees [pre-approved by the Defense Department](https://theintercept.com/2025/12/12/venezuela-boat-strikes-video-press-coverage/). This prompted most media outlets, except for the right-wing MAGA-friendly One America News Network, to surrender their press passes.

Trump has also targeted specific media outlets and individual journalists by [barring](https://pressfreedomtracker.us/all-incidents/trump-bans-three-outlets-from-white-house-access-citing-fake-news/) them from the White House or Air Force One, though a federal court judge has since paused the bans, cautioning against possible violations of the First Amendment.

The Intercept and FPF’s lawsuits arrive days after Hegseth narrowly [survived an impeachment attempt](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/10/hegseth-no-impeachment-house-vote/) over his [handling of the Iran war](https://theintercept.com/2026/11/05/midterms-hegseth-impeach-pressure-massie-military/). The effort, led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., and backed by Democrats, failed to garner enough votes to impeach Hegseth.

[Related “Trump Has Appointed Himself Judge, Jury, and Executioner”](https://theintercept.com/2025/12/12/venezuela-boat-strikes-video-press-coverage/)

In addition to the war on Iran, incoming Democratic members of Congress, along with human rights groups, seek to hold Hegseth accountable for his [bloody airstrike campaign](https://theintercept.com/collections/license-to-kill/) on boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean, in which the U.S. has killed more than 240 civilians, and his overseeing of the U.S. invasion of [Venezuela](https://theintercept.com/2026/01/05/trump-venezuela-war/).

articleBody:
*This episode is

Not many people know that Stable Diffusion is why I went fulltime into AI (I aptly titled [Multiverse, not Metaverse](https://latent.space/p/multiverse-not-metaverse/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) to call out Zuck’s mistaken investment). It turns out that **Dustin Podell**also had the same aha moment - quitting his day job when the model came out. But we took very different paths… I stuck to what I knew in human content creation, and Dustin immersed deep into AI content creation with**Andreas Blattmann**, co-inventor of Latent Diffusion and the rest of the world-leading imagegen crew at Stability AI. Stability fell apart, but [Anj Midha](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dCX4PE2HxMs&t=1s&utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) helped the core group spin out to BFL, which immediately built an incredible new imagegen model in the Flux series.**But why are they now going into video and world models?**

Andreas gives an example you can try with one hand. If somebody tosses you a ball, your hand starts moving before the ball reaches you. You can do that without being able to write down the trajectory. When he talks about building **visual intelligence**, that’s the kind of knowledge he means. A still can show you where the ball is. A video shows you how it got there. The sound of impact can tell you when it hit something, even if the camera missed the contact. That’s BFL’s argument for training FLUX 3 on the three signals together. [BFL’s FLUX 3 release](https://bfl.ai/blog/flux-3?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

*The horse in motion is one of the FLUX 3 examples we show in the intro. The audio examples are worth playing with the sound on.* [FLUX 3 Video](https://bfl.ai/blog/flux-3-video?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

## What a moving camera teaches you

Suppose the camera starts in front of a person and pans around them. At some point the model owes you the back of their head. Andreas thinks ordinary two-dimensional video contains a great deal of evidence about what objects look like from other angles. That doesn’t settle whether a model “understands physics,” a point we go back and forth on. It does give you a much better test than asking whether one frame looks convincing.

There’s a good engineering example late in the episode. Sharpen each frame of a clip independently and each frame might look terrific. Hit play and the extra detail can shimmer, because the upscaler made a slightly different decision every time. BFL derives its video upscaler from the same FLUX 3 backbone. Temporal consistency matters even when all the user asked for was a higher-resolution file.

## What’s worth spending training compute on?

One of the questions I had for them was whether autoregression was taking over image generation. Andreas gives the other side its due. An autoregressive model can learn from all the tokens in a training example at once. On the diffusion side, the team can distill a long sampling process down to a handful of steps. Which advantage matters depends on whether you’re paying to train the model or waiting for an image to finish.

Dustin’s early Kontext experiment is a nice example of how they decide where to invest. He suspected an image model that could *draw* a dog wearing a hat already knew something about where hats go. He and a colleague collected a small set of photos labeled with relationships. A training run of a few hours got the model to put a logo on a shirt. It was rough, but it was enough to take to the next offsite. The team then spent months on the data and the model. [FLUX Kontext examples](https://bfl.ai/models/flux-kontext?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

My favorite user story comes near the end. People were feeding FLUX old, degraded family photos, restoring them, then showing the pictures to their families. Dustin says he hadn’t predicted that use. After talking about preserving somebody’s identity across edits and across frames, it’s a lovely example of who actually notices if you get it right.

## Show notes

- BFL explains what a still image, a moving camera and a soundtrack each contribute during training. [FLUX 3 launch and research overview](https://bfl.ai/blog/flux-3?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)
- Watch and listen to the results of generating video and sound together. [FLUX 3 Video demos](https://bfl.ai/blog/flux-3-video?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)
- See how the lab teaches a model to make a requested change while preserving the rest of an image. [FLUX Kontext examples](https://bfl.ai/models/flux-kontext?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)
- Andreas Blattmann co-created Stable Diffusion and co-invented the latent diffusion method behind it. [Guest bio](https://raais.co/speakers-2025-andreas-blattmann-black-forest-labs?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) · [Original research](https://ommer-lab.com/research/latent-diffusion-models/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)
- Dustin Podell led FLUX Kontext and was the lead author of SDXL. [Dustin’s project credits](https://dustinpodell.com/about/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) · [FLUX Kontext](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.15742?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv) · [SDXL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01952?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)
- The first Latent Space essay grew out of the Stable Diffusion release. [Multiverse, not Metaverse](https://latent.space/p/multiverse-not-metaverse/?utm_source=latent.space&utm_medium=ainews&utm_campaign=lsbeehiiv)

articleBody:
From an early mishmash of chaotic lines and misspelled words to the loose lilt of a signature scribbled for decades, “Paper Trail” is a moving animation that shows the evolution of a young mind and what we can glean from a life through notes and lists. The latest project by [Don Hertzfeldt](https://www.bitterfilms.com/), the short film follows the protagonist Steven Richardson as he makes his first marks, learns to write his name, doodles, and later completes the perfunctory math problems of elementary school. We witness his cursive lessons and adolescent love letters to a girl named Lindsey before observing grocery lists and remnants of his professional life.

Based in Austin, Texas, Hertzfeldt is known for his poetic animations that harness the indelible intimacy of hand-drawn scenes. “Paper Trail” has been on the festival circuit where it’s garnered top honors at Annecy, Sundance, SXSW, and many others. The film is available for streaming for a limited-timed on [Vimeo](https://vimeo.com/donhertzfeldt), along with more of Hertzfeldt’s work.

title: On this day in space! Nov. 16, 1974: The giant Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico broadcasts humanity's 1st interstellar message
subtitle: 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

articleBody:
On Nov. 16, 1974, humans sent their first message to the stars in an attempt to contact extraterrestrials.

They did this using what was then the largest radio telescope in the world, located at the [Arecibo Observatory](https://www.space.com/20984-arecibo-observatory.html) in Puerto Rico. A group of scientists led by Frank Drake and Carl Sagan sent their message to the M13 [star cluster](https://www.space.com/star-clusters). The message was written in binary code and contained information about human DNA.

It also included figures of a human, [the solar system](https://www.space.com/16080-solar-system-planets.html) and the Arecibo telescope. The idea was that if any aliens were to receive the signal and figure out how to decode it, they would know where it came from. Because M13 is 25,000 light-years away, it will take 25,000 years for any M13 aliens to hear our message — if they are even out there.

(Image credit: SETI)

## Why it mattered

The Arecibo message is only one of several messages intended for extraterrestrials, but this signal sent from Puerto Rico in 1974 was humanity's first intentional olive branch to the stars. At the time, it was the most powerful broadcast ever beamed into space, according to the SETI Institute.

"The broadcast was particularly powerful because it used Arecibo's megawatt transmitter attached to its 305 meter antenna," [SETI wrote of the broadcast](https://www.seti.org/research/seti-101/project-phoenix/arecibo/) in a project over. "The emission was equivalent to a 20 trillion watt omnidirectional broadcast, and would be detectable by a SETI experiment just about anywhere in the galaxy, assuming a receiving antenna similar in size to Arecibo's."

The message was designed by astronomy professor [Frank Drake](https://www.space.com/28665-seti-astronomer-frank-drake-interview.html) of Cornell University (who also developed the famed [Drake Equation](https://www.space.com/25219-drake-equation.html) for alien life), as well as Cornnell graduate students Richard Isaacman and Linda May, and Arecibo staff member James Walker, with input from astronomer Carl Sagan and others, [according to Cornell University](https://news.cornell.edu/stories/1999/11/25th-anniversary-first-attempt-phone-et-0).

The message included 1,679 bits that were arranged in 73 lines of 23 characters per line, all prime numbers, with the broadcast lasting less than 3 minutes, according to SETI.

As of 2026, the message should have traveled about 52 light-years (1 [light-year](https://www.space.com/light-year.html) is the distance light travels in a year), with 24,948 light-years to go before reaching star cluster M13.

The Arecibo message may have been the first message of its kind, but it wasn't the last. We have also included messages on several spacecraft, such as Pioneer and Voyager. NASA and Paul McCartney also [b eamed a performance of "Across the Universe"](https://www.space.com/4903-nasa-takes-beatles-universe-literally.html) in 2008.

Want more space history? Check out our[full On This Day In Space Story archive](https://www.space.com/tag/on-this-day-in-space) and watch our[On This Day In Space videos on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLCE-SVF9BSTdloyi4P9TmQVTp9Q2zTb27).

subtitle: Im Laufe des Tages hatten wir euch bereits auf Gerüchte zum Kamerasystem des iPhone 20 Pro aufmerksam gemacht.

articleBody:
Im Laufe des Tages hatten wir euch bereits auf Gerüchte zum Kamerasystem des iPhone 20 Pro aufmerksam gemacht. Nun gibt es das nächste Appetithäppchen. Das Unternehmen aus Cupertino könnte für das 20-jährige iPhone-Jubiläum im Herbst 2027 ein besonders auffälliges Redesign planen. Nach einem neuen Bericht des chinesischen Leakers Fixed Focus Digital soll sich das iPhone 20 Pro beim Gehäuse am iPhone Air orientieren. Allerdings plant Apple offenbar deutlich stärker gewölbte Glasflächen, die sich über alle vier Seiten des Geräts erstrecken.

Fotocredit: Apple

## Mischung aus iPhone X und iPhone Air

Glaubt man den Informationen des [Leakers](https://weibo.com/5821279480/5365097321201793), so wird Apple dasselbe Glasmaterial verwenden, das bereits beim iPhone Air zum Einsatz kommt. Durch eine stärkere Krümmung an Vorder- und Rückseite entsteht ein rundum abgerundetes Erscheinungsbild. Ein schmaler, glänzender Metallrahmen verbindet weiterhin die beiden Glasflächen.

Das Design könnte eine Kombination aus zwei bisherigen iPhone-Modellen darstellen. Während die schlanke Bauweise und die Glasverarbeitung an das iPhone Air erinnern, weckt die stärkere Rundung Erinnerungen an das iPhone X aus dem Jahr 2017.

Bereits im August hatte derselbe Leaker [berichtet](https://www.macerkopf.de/2026/08/24/gebogene-glasdesign-jubilaeums-iphone-air/), dass Apple Fertigungsanlagen des iPhone Air für die Produktion des Jubiläumsmodells angepasst habe. Die Änderungen sollen eine dünnere Konstruktion, eine bessere Wärmeableitung und niedrigere Herstellungskosten ermöglichen.

[Auch Apple-Insider Mark Gurman](https://www.macerkopf.de/2026/09/05/iphone20-geruecht-redesign-iphone-x/) hatte bereits von einem weitgehend aus Glas bestehenden iPhone mit gewölbten Displayrändern berichtet. Demnach sollen die Glasflächen von vorne und hinten in die Gehäuseseiten übergehen. Zusätzlich werden besonders schmale Displayränder erwartet.

### Größtes Redesign seit dem iPhone X?

Das Jubiläumsmodell könnte damit die umfassendste optische Überarbeitung der Pro-Reihe seit dem iPhone X darstellen. Neben dem neuen Gehäuse werden weitere technische Neuerungen erwartet. Spekuliert wird unter anderem über einen Apple eigener Kamerasensor mit LOFIC-Technologie und ein neuer A21 Pro Chip.

Am meisten hilft eine monatliche Spende: Mit ihr können wir Recherchen planen, die Monate dauern. Mit deiner Dauerspende können wir auch dann dranbleiben, wenn andere keine Kraft mehr haben.

**Uns fehlen aktuell noch 477.000 Euro, damit wir unsere Arbeit im kommenden Jahr fortsetzen können.** Wenn wir mehr zusammen bekommen, können wir unser Team ausbauen. Sichere jetzt mit deiner Spende unabhängigen Journalismus für alle!

Die Demokratie wankt. Rechtsradikale greifen nach der Macht und wollen Grundrechte brennen sehen. Die Bundesregierung gießt Öl ins Feuer: Sie rüstet den Überwachungsstaat auf, schränkt die Transparenz ein und schneidet der Zivilgesellschaft die Luft ab.

Wir treten diesem autoritären Rollback entgegen. Wir schauen genau hin, wenn Freiheit unter Druck gerät. Mit investigativen Recherchen, Analysen, Leaks und einem langen Atem kämpfen wir für die Grund- und Freiheitsrechte aller und den gesellschaftlichen Zusammenhalt.

title: This Supernova is 50 Million Light Years Away, But That's Close Enough For Astronomers
subtitle: A new supernova has been detected in a spiral galaxy about 50 million light years away.
feedText: That's close enough for detatiled follow-up observations, which have already begun. It's a type Ia supernova, meaning it's an exploding white dwarf rather than a massive star ending its life in a core-collapse detonation. Astronomers will watch as its light fades and changes over the next days, months, and years to track the changes and learn more about these standard candles. It's close enough for astrophotographers to get in on the action, too.

It's a type Ia supernova, meaning it's an exploding white dwarf rather than a massive star ending its life in a core-collapse detonation. Astronomers will watch as its light fades and changes over the next days, months, and years to track the changes and learn more about these standard candles. It's close enough for astrophotographers to get in on the action, too.

title: Apple’s Second 27.3 Developer Beta Adds Face Unlock for iPhone Duo, New Mac Privacy Controls, and More
subtitle: Apple’s developer betas this cycle have been packed with more features than usual and today’s second developer beta for 27.3 is no different.
feedText: Let’s dig in. The iPhone Duo gets a pair of changes in the latest developer beta that are likely to be crowd pleasers when 27.3 is released to the public. articleBody:
Apple’s developer betas this cycle have been packed with more features than usual and today’s second developer beta for 27.3 is no different. Let’s dig in.

The iPhone Duo gets a pair of changes in the latest developer beta that are likely to be crowd pleasers when 27.3 is released to the public. First, the Duo will be able to unlock quickly using the front-facing camera when it has been recently unlocked with Touch ID or a user’s passcode. The feature can be found in Settings -> Touch ID & Passcode and [according to Max Weinbach](https://x.com/mweinbach/status/2122397014373622020?a=GK5cng3NTtWB2uFGDUI&s=20), it uses the Secure Exclave to process the image used, which is how the HomeView works, too.

Touch ID will still be needed to use Apple Pay and access passwords. Additionally, Touch ID will be needed after roughly 45 minutes.

Second, if you want your iPhone Duo to lock when you fold it, like an iPad or Mac laptop, you’ll be able to turn that on, too, under Settings -> Display & Brightness. This isn’t something I expect I’ll turn on myself, but I know a lot of MacStories readers have wanted this, so I’m glad to see it added as an option.

Also, you may recall that Apple gave developers a vague heads-up about changes coming to Full Disk Access, which I [wrote about at the time](https://www.macstories.net/linked/apple-announces-plan-to-impose-new-full-disk-access-controls-on-mac-developers/), and we discussed on [AppStories](https://www.macstories.net/podcasts/appstories/505/) recently. Today we got more information on what that means on [Apple’s developer website](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=oqng0zjk):

> In macOS 27.3 beta 2 today, we’re introducing increased transparency and more granular options for two of the APIs: Device Control and Data Access, and Full Disk Access. Before granting an app such extraordinary access, users should understand that it puts all of the data on their Mac at risk. These changes are designed to help them do that and to empower them to make informed decisions about their own data and privacy.

In practice, this means that macOS 27.3 will split “Device Control and Data Access” in Settings into a two-part system that divides the world into Accessibility features for assistive technologies and “System & App Protection Override,” which lets users pick which apps an overriding app can control. In addition, [Apple says](https://developer.apple.com/news/?id=oqng0zjk) the changes will include:

> A single method for granting permissions by selecting the requesting app from a list
> Guidance to encourage users to grant access to just the specific apps (for System & App Protection Override) or folders (for Full Disk Access) that are required for their workflows
> Increased visibility into the wide range of data apps will receive access to or control over if full permissions are granted
> The option for users to configure apps to ask every time they require access
> A transparency indicator when a requesting app is controlling another app using System & App Protection Override

Also, it’s worth noting that [Chance Miller of 9to5Mac says](https://x.com/chancehmiller/status/2122409697303241201?s=46) that Full Disk Access will remain available but that users will be steered toward using the new system.

I haven’t had a chance to try this yet, but it sounds like a reasonable solution that divides permissions into more sensible categories with better control and understanding over what privileges are being granted.

Siri is gaining the ability to see beyond the part of a webpage that is visible in Safari. Whatever’s below the fold of the page will be accessible whether you’re asking for a summary or requesting specific information at the end of a long page.

The Apple TV app is adding support for video podcast episodes, too. The feature will be available on the Apple TV 4K and supported iPhones, iPads, Macs, CarPlay-enabled vehicles, and smart TVs. I know you’ve always wanted to watch AppStories on your 90-inch TV, and soon, you can. Technology is incredible!

The puzzles in Apple News+ are popular in my household, and they’re coming to more countries. Apple News’ crosswords, Sudoku, Emoji Game, and more are coming to the Australian, UK, and French-Canadian editions of Apple News+ when 27.3 is released.

Of these, the Face Unlock feature is the one I’m most eager to try, but I’m also glad to see that Apple doesn’t appear to have made granting app and data privileges to apps too onerous. One thing’s for sure, beta season isn’t so much a season these days as it is a revolving door, and I love it.
