articleBody:
### 🚀 SpaceX catches returning Starship for first time

[↗ Primärquelle: foxbusiness.com](https://www.foxbusiness.com/technology/spacex-makes-history-starship-spacecraft-caught-launch-tower-first-time)

- SpaceX pulled off a first on Saturday, catching its Starship spacecraft with the giant mechanical arms at its Texas launch tower as the vehicle returned from orbit, a key step toward building a fully reusable rocket.
- The catch happened on the 15th test flight, roughly 22 hours after Starship lifted off on Friday, during which the spacecraft released 26 Starlink satellites and circled Earth 14 times before landing back at Starbase.
- SpaceX missed its goal of recovering both stages after the Super Heavy booster's engines shut off early during descent and it exploded over the Gulf, an outcome engineers are now investigating.

### 📣 165,000 sign letter to reinstate Nvidia's Huang

[↗ Primärquelle: cnbc.com](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/11/16/nvidia-jensen-huang-return-tech.html)

- Elon Musk and more than 165,000 people have signed an open letter urging Nvidia's board to reinstate Jensen Huang as chief, just days after he resigned from the trillion-dollar chip company he co-founded.
- The signatories include Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, Y Combinator's Garry Tan, and Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, while over 7,500 of them identified as Nvidia employees, about 18% of the company's workforce.
- Huang resigned on Thursday after revelations of extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China, and US treasury secretary Scott Bessent said on Sunday that Nvidia needs an outside chief and a "dramatic shake-up".

### 💥 Amazon loses 40 satellites in failed rocket launch

[↗ Primärquelle: geekwire.com](https://www.geekwire.com/2026/amazon-loses-40-leo-satellites-as-ula-vulcan-launch-failure-deals-setback-to-tech-giants-starlink-rival/)

- A United Launch Alliance Vulcan rocket failed about 10 minutes after liftoff yesterday, destroying 40 satellites for Amazon Leo, the Seattle company's planned rival to SpaceX's Starlink internet service.
- The failure, ULA's first total mission loss since 2006, came during the Centaur upper stage burn, after the solid boosters and Blue Origin BE-4 first-stage engines appeared to work normally; ULA says it doesn't yet know the cause.
- Vulcan was the first of 38 launches Amazon bought and is meant to carry over 1,500 satellites; the mishap delays the next Vulcan flight, though an Ariane 6 launch with 36 satellites is targeted for November 23.

### 🇺🇸 US blocks China from renting AI chips abroad

[↗ Primärquelle: techcrunch.com](https://techcrunch.com/2026/11/16/us-tightens-ai-chip-export-controls-to-deter-chinese-companies-from-accessing-compute-remotely/)

- The Trump administration is rolling out new export controls today to stop Chinese firms from sidestepping U.S. restrictions by remotely tapping AI chips and data centers located in other countries.
- Under the interim rule, the Commerce Department will require export licenses for any data center or network able to supply more than 12 million TPP, roughly 750 Nvidia H100 or H200 chips, that may serve companies in China.
- The rule targets the D:5 group of 22 embargoed countries, adds licensing for chip transfers to Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, and scraps the Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule from January 2025.

### 🍎 Apple launches study on trust in health AI

- Apple has started a year-long study, built with the clinical AI tool OpenEvidence, to learn what makes Americans trust health AI chatbots and how well people understand the answers those tools give.
- Up to 200,000 US users can join the Apple Health AI Usage Study, rating responses in monthly surveys, though participants must be at least 21 and own an iPhone 15 Pro or newer running iOS 26.
- Study data won't train AI models, and queries are made anonymous before going to a third-party cloud, where OpenEvidence deletes them after 24 hours; people may also choose to share HealthKit data like sleep and heart rate.

### 🧠 Alibaba's Qwen4-Max cuts task costs 60%

[↗ Primärquelle: csoonline.com](https://www.csoonline.com/article/4249015/alibaba-touts-62-lower-task-costs-with-qwen4-max-adds-cyber-safeguards-2.html)

- Alibaba's new flagship model Qwen4-Max completes professional tasks for 62% less than the version before it, dropping the average cost from $4.43 to $1.67 per task, according to the company's own Work360 benchmark.
- The 2.4-trillion-parameter model activates about 71 billion parameters per token, down from 95 billion, and uses 35% fewer tokens, with new prices of $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens.
- Alibaba also filtered training data to keep defensive cybersecurity skills while removing offensive ones, but analysts warned the split needs outside testing and said buyers should measure the real cost of finished tasks, not token prices.

- AI, work from home, and the young-graduate job market [↗ stripeeconomics.com](https://www.stripeeconomics.com/p/ai-work-from-home-and-the-young-graduate)

### 🧰 Trending tools

**Cookie Away:** rejects cookie banners automatically, opening settings to disable tracking when no reject button exists, with verified results across 69 sites [↗ cookieaway.com](https://cookieaway.com)

**Cal.com v7:** open-source scheduling platform that lets people book meetings with you through shareable links, handling availability and time zones automatically. [↗ producthunt.com](https://producthunt.com/products/cal)

**Zoom Slides:** create, edit, present, and share presentations in one tool, streamlining deck-building from first draft through final delivery and collaboration. [↗ aisuite.zoom.com](https://aisuite.zoom.com/slides)

**WHOOP Humans:** lets you follow specific friends and family to view their shared sleep, recovery, strain, and activity data through direct, request-based connections. [↗ whoop.com](https://whoop.com/us/en/thelocker/meet-whoop-humans-follow-friends-capture-moments-go-deeper-into-data)

**TK by Medium:** a publishing platform for reading and writing stories, letting you reach readers without first building a following or mailing list. [↗ tk.xyz](https://tk.xyz)

**Blender 5.3:** free, open-source 3D suite covering modeling, rigging, animation, simulation, rendering, compositing, motion tracking, video editing, and 2D animation in one package. [↗ producthunt.com](https://producthunt.com/products/blender)

### 📚 Trending papers & reports

> **Hootsuite:** they asked the teams actually winning on social what is working right now, and published all 17 trends in a free report. Download the report

> **Adversarial camera attacks** can fool a self-driving car's vehicle-tracking system by subtly tampering with its video feed, cutting tracking accuracy from about 55 percent to as low as 15 percent and sometimes worse. [↗ arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17505)

> **AI video tools** face emissions rising nearly seventy-five-fold by 2030 under continued growth despite efficiency gains, while holding usage flat would cut emissions by about two-fifths, a warning that scale itself is the problem. [↗ arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.17938)

> **Healthcare AI spending** grew 2.5x to 3.7 billion in 2026, surpassing legal and finance combined, as Menlo Ventures finds the market shifting from commoditized note-taking toward complex clinical and drug-discovery workflows. [↗ menlovc.com](https://menlovc.com/perspective/2026-the-state-of-ai-in-healthcare)

articleBody:
## WAYS OF GROWING EXAMINES BOTANICAL BIODIVERSITY AND BIO-DESIGN

On view at the Gallery of the Faculty of Fine Arts at the University of Lisbon (FBAUL) through November 28th, 2026, Ways of Growing / Modos de crescer presents works by 20 artists, designers, and researchers examining the intersection of plant biodiversity and **[material](https://www.designboom.com/tag/materials/)**experimentation. Serving as the culmination of the two-year Free Radicals research initiative, led by Haenke (Czech Republic) alongside partners in Portugal, Spain, Armenia, Hungary, and Germany, the**[exhibition](https://www.designboom.com/tag/exhibitions/)**originates from three 2025 field residencies conducted in Galicia’s Courel mountains, a permaculture farm in central**[Portugal](https://www.designboom.com/tag/architecture-in-portugal/)**, and northern Armenia’s Lori Mountains.

all images ©Sandra Teixeira / Free Radicals

- ## BIO-MATERIALS AND BOTANICAL CHEMISTRY ANCHOR EXHIBITION WORKS

Rather than treating flora solely as passive raw matter, the exhibited works engage botanical organisms, agricultural byproducts, and local ecologies as active design agents. Material and technical investigations span cyanotypes printed on kombucha-derived bacterial cellulose and toned with plant extracts, bio-composites pairing traditional Portuguese crochet with living mycelium, and textiles woven from chestnut-dyed linen. Additional installations integrate botanical chemistry and digital hardware, including olfactory sculptures formulated from eucalyptus ash and essential oils, plant-based analog film processing, acoustic transmission through organic substrates, and a multimedia system linking historic Armenian herbaria with Raspberry Pi microcomputers. Inaugurated during FBAUL’s 190th anniversary, **[the exhibition](https://www.freeradicals.space/)** coincides with the release of Free Radicals: Attuning to Plants in Creative Practices (Onomatopee), a publication edited by Sasha Střelcová and Linsey Rendell compiling methodologies from 70 practitioners across design, ecology, and material research.

Elena Falomo’s research-led installation combines field recordings, geographical artefacts and storytelling to question which landscapes are prioritised in responses to climate change

Eleonora Edreva’s textile-based poem is woven from vintage linen, chestnut dyes, local language and sound

Ivana Papić uses ecological fiction to question invasive-species narratives in her experimental video essay imagining a love story between a native chestnut tree and an introduced mimosa

Alejandra Díaz-Guerra Acedo’s bio-based textile experiment combines traditional Portuguese crochet with living mycelium, allowing fungi to decompose cotton fabrics buried in contrasting soils

Maria Ilieva’s olfactory compositions trace the lifecycle of eucalyptus from fresh foliage and wildfire to industrial pulp processing and paper production

food artist and chef Aly Beveridge explores how our proximity to land and ingredients create a bodily intimacy that allows us to reconsider our relationship to food

Adam Kvaček’s performative walk explored the familiar language of recreational tourism to investigate Portugal’s industrial eucalyptus landscapes

Ways of Growing / Modos de crescer explores the intersections between plant biodiversity and creative practice

Ricardo Nugra’s sound sculpture translates the material traces of wildfire and deforestation into tactile vibrations via eucalyptus ash, pine resin, field recordings, and bone-conduction technology

Free Radicals is a two-year European research project exploring the intersections between plant biodiversity and artistic practice

the exhibition is on display at the Gallery of the Faculty of Fine Arts, University of Lisbon (FBAUL)

published by Onomatopee, Free Radicals: Attuning to Plants in Creative Practices is a collectively assembled toolkit; part manifesto, part gathering space

**program:** [Free Radicals](https://www.freeradicals.space/) | [@freeradicals.space](https://www.instagram.com/freeradicals.space)

title: How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096
subtitle:

How do you invent the future?
feedText: This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time for New Scientist’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. articleBody:
Fatih Aktas/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images

How do you invent the future? This isn’t a question that I had ever had to consider until I [set out to imagine what the world would be like in 70 years’ time](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2597572-this-is-what-the-world-will-be-like-in-2096-a-special-report-from-the-future/) for *New Scientist* ’s 70th anniversary. As a lifelong sci-fi nerd, I have read and watched loads of material that could have served as inspiration. But this being *New Scientist*, I wanted to make sure that I was as grounded in real science and technology as possible – while acknowledging that no prediction of the future is ever correct.

I began by asking my colleagues on the magazine for their ideas about the future and then attempted to corral this sci-fi smorgasbord into something resembling an outline of a self-consistent narrative. Part of the problem in imagining many different futures is that they contradict themselves – you can’t have the war-torn AI dystopia of *Terminator* alongside the [utopia of Star Trek](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2587667-as-star-trek-turns-60-its-not-too-late-to-discover-the-seminal-series/).

I wanted both hope and realism in my future, so I decided to look at how the scientific literature handles the end of the century. One of the most obvious forecasts is for climate change, where we have a pretty good idea about what might happen in 2096, under a range of scenarios, because it all boils down to atmospheric physics that we can model. Of course, which of these scenarios we end up with is all too dependent on human politics, so the science alone couldn’t guide me. I also turned to [population projections](https://www.newscientist.com/topic/population/), which, for the most part, are locked in based on current population trends. The idea that the end of the century will be the first time we are living in a world of falling populations became a fascinating strand in the final piece.

The biggest problem I faced was how to deal with AI. I am not confident making predictions on this topic even just a few years in advance – as I’ve written previously, [my views on AI have evolved between the release of ChatGPT in 2022 and now](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2516907-why-i-have-changed-my-mind-about-ai-and-you-should-too/), so how could I possibly predict what would happen by the time we got to 2096? Furthermore, there was a risk that AI could come to dominate the piece, crowding out everything else. There is a graph I often think about, [published by the Financial Times](https://www.ft.com/content/60dfa917-c5e6-4b9b-9cdb-a30692a29527?syn-25a6b1a6=1) under the headline “AI could end scarcity, end humanity – or boost [GDP] growth by 0.2 percentage points”. I knew that, to preserve any meaningful narrative, I had to restrict AI to this boring middle option, so I invented an AI-fuelled financial crisis that would see us place limits on the technology. I have no idea if such an event is likely to happen, but it seems to me to be the only way to preserve a future that remains comprehensible to us today.

I spoke to dozens of experts to help inform this piece, expecting them to contradict each other in ways that were both helpful and confounding, and they did. But what I found most interesting is how little interdisciplinary forecasting there is across science. For example, attempts to predict future public health trends are only just starting to consider how climate change will interact with the diseases and medical conditions we face. Meanwhile, many of the people I spoke to hadn’t deeply considered how AI would affect the evolution of their chosen discipline.

[How I used evidence and imagination to write an account of the world in 2096 Writing about what the world will be like in 70 years could have been simply an exercise in fiction. But by grounding the story in hard evidence, I got real insights](https://www.newscientist.com/article/2598686-how-i-used-evidence-and-imagination-to-write-an-account-of-the-world-in-2096/)

In weaving all this together, one of the most surprising things I arrived at was the idea of expanding the legal concept of personhood. Looking at how our attitudes towards both animals and artificial intelligence are changing today, it seemed to me that this was a possibility, so I created the International Treaty on Non-Human Personhood. Its existence in the story had a number of interesting downstream effects, and I kept finding different ways for non-human people to influence the world. Again, this is a big bet, but I think not an unreasonable one.

One thing I couldn’t escape from in writing this piece is the idea that I and probably all of the people I interviewed won’t be around to see what comes to pass. I would be 110 years old in 2096 – not impossible, especially given the advances in medicine I describe in the piece, but still unlikely. In some ways, 70 years from now is the perfect amount of time to forecast the future, being just outside most adults’ expected lifespan. We can never know what will really happen – we can only imagine.

articleBody:
Mona Chalabi is a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist, and as much as it shows across her incredible body of visual data reporting, she has always kept her eye on another prize entirely. I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole.

The culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, *Ten Lives* breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work itself. Chalabi brings a refreshing integrity and playful approach to reporting unflinchingly on the genocide in Palestine, the horrors of the healthcare system, and massive wealth inequality. While she insists her work isn’t “fine art,” it’s perhaps the purest example of what art should do: challenge our ways of seeing. She’s also uncommonly funny, humble, and perceptive. (Can you tell I’m a fan?)

Class is also at the center of photographer Mark Alice Durant’s memoiristic book, which critic Melissa Holbrook Pierson likens to Rainer Maria Rilke’s *Letters to a Young Poet* for our dystopian world of 2026. Other books in this edition similarly respond to the Orwellian state of art and power. Nitasha Dhillon and Amin Husain, both scholars and activists, have organized protests against the Museum of Modern Art in 2021, the Whitney Biennial in 2019, and the Guggenheim Abu Dhabi in 2015, among other instances of artwashing. They penned a joint review of Italian curator and organizer Marco Baravalle’s book *The Battleground of Art: Radical Curating in the Crisis of Neoliberalism*, a toolkit for seeing through the mainstream art world’s undermining of political movements and building sustainable alternatives.

Critic Carolina A. Miranda, meanwhile, takes up two new books by East Los Angeles artist Guadalupe Rosales, who came up in a community of Chicano kids raised in the 1990s amid uprisings and political action. Miranda writes that the anthology Rosales edited, as well as her blended memoir and photo book, perfectly encapsulate “the ways she engages the stories of others even as she tells her own.” A wise observation to carry with us as we face the week ahead; more of the latest in art book reviews and news below.

*—Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books*

[Mona Chalabi Paints a Picture of Class Inequality](https://hyperallergic.com/mona-chalabi-paints-a-picture-of-class-inequality/)

## In the News

- M. John Harrison [won the Booker prize](https://www.theguardian.com/books/2026/nov/09/m-john-harrison-the-end-of-everything-wins-2026-booker-prize?ref=hyperallergic.com) for The End of Everything, and readers and literary critics are split. Some are thrilled to see a science fiction title nab the award, a first in its nearly six-decade history. But the shortlist included a few undeniable favorites, like Jamaican novelist Marlon James’s The Disappearers, and the prize committee has a tendency to favor White, male authors (shocker!). I plan to read both and make up my mind after; let me know your thoughts in the meantime.
- Natalie Renganeschi is joining the [Women’s Studio Workshop](https://hyperallergic.com/print-center-and-womens-studio-workshop-name-new-leaders/), a center for printmaking, bookbinding, and other paper-related arts, as executive director.
- After five years, Michelle T. Boone is retiring from her post as president and CEO of the [Poetry Foundation](https://www.publishersweekly.com/pw/newsbrief/index.html?record=6098&ref=hyperallergic.com).
- A Mario Vargas Llosa biography that was in the works for 13 years got [dropped](https://www.thetimes.com/world/europe/article/penguin-book-biography-scathing-nobel-laureate-mario-vargas-llosa-0k66fx903?ref=hyperallergic.com) by Penguin for being what it deemed too critical of the Peruvian author.
- A Truman Capote estate auction has a few odd items up for grabs, namely [the ashes of his dog Maggie](https://lithub.com/you-can-now-buy-the-ashes-of-truman-capotes-dog/?ref=hyperallergic.com). The wonders of auction houses never cease.

## Required Reading

- Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy, whose memoir was nominated for a National Book Award, has a [must-read essay](https://www.newyorker.com/books/page-turner/i-am-a-2026-national-book-award-finalist-the-us-denied-my-visa?ref=hyperallergic.com) out about the US’s denial of the visitor visa he requested to attend the ceremony in New York City this Wednesday. [ New Yorker ]
- If you’ve ever wanted to create a [time capsule](https://longreads.com/2026/11/05/time-capsules-ashley-stimpson/?ref=hyperallergic.com), Ashley Stimpson has some thoughts. She writes about the history of the practice, the slim odds that a time capsule will ever be found, and why you should make one anyway. [ Longreads ]
- During her pregnancy, filmmaker Siraad Dirshe found solace in books like Sasha Bonét’s The Waterbearers, a reminder of the need to [archive, narrate, and preserve stories of Black motherhood](https://lithub.com/what-we-lose-when-we-dont-archive-black-motherhood/?ref=hyperallergic.com). [ Literary Hub ]

## What We’re Reading

**Lakshmi Rivera Amin, associate editor, books**
As I rejoin the queue for the Valeria Luiselli book that expired on my Kindle — the Brooklyn Public Library doesn’t play about digital loans — I’ve added a romance novel to my rotation: Ali Hazelwood’s [The Love Hypothesis](http://bookshop.org/a/539/9780593336823?ref=hyperallergic.com) (2021). It’s predictable, it’s corny, and it’s just STEM enough to make me feel like I’m learning something about scientific research funding and early-detection cancer biomarkers. Truly the perfect holiday-season read.

**Rebecca Schiffman, associate editor**
I just got a copy of Min Jin Lee’s highly anticipated [American Hagwon](http://bookshop.org/a/539/9781538752036?ref=hyperallergic.com) and 50 pages in, I’m already hooked. The third in her *Diaspora Quartet*, it follows a Korean family doing their best to assimilate and find their place at a *hagwon*, or cram school.

## From the Archive

[An Art Thief’s Tale of Love and Seduction](https://hyperallergic.com/art-thief-stephane-breitwieser-tale-of-love-and-seduction-michael-finkel/)

body: I sat down with her earlier this fall at Christopher Park across from the Stonewall Inn, a site of protest and resistance, to talk about her new book and her career as a whole. The culmination of six years of research, interviews, and illustration, Ten Lives breaks the silence around class in her characteristic visual style. To me, it’s a reflection of her principled approach to journalism and storytelling that feel utterly lost in a world where self-promotion, access, and branding can matter more than the work…

articleBody:
**We’re a few weeks into a reboot of our [Beautiful News](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/) project from a few years ago. Refreshed. Revitalised. Re-visualised.**

Once more, every day for a year, we are surfacing and visualising some of the **amazing, progressive and positive things happening around the world**. Trends and events and innovations we can’t always see when fixated on the negativity of the news.

We’ve spruced and updated some of data-visualisations from the original collection, as well as adding 160 more stories to be released over the next weeks, months, year and beyond!

Every graphic is of course underpinned by [open datasets](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/data/) to support full **evidence-based optimism.**

Swing by and join [our weekly newsletter](https://beautifulnews.myflodesk.com/newsletter) or daily on [the website](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/), or social channels of your choosing: [Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/beautifulnews.daily), [Twitter/X](https://x.com/beautiful__news), [Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/beautifulnewsdaily/), [Threads](https://www.threads.com/@beautifulnews.daily).

## Some of my favourite graphics and stories so far

» [34 Countries Now Generate 80% or More of Their Electricity from Renewables](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3021-countries-electricity-renewables/)

» [Tons of new vaccines are in the pipeline](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/524-new-vaccines/)

» [Polio is very nearly wiped out](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3037-polio-wiped-out/)

» [The Cost of Renewable Energy is Plunging](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/586-cost-renewables-falling/)

» [The EU Gender Pay Gap is (slowly) Decreasing](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/3030-eu-gender-pay-gap/)

» [Everyone, Everywhere, is Living Longer](https://informationisbeautiful.net/beautifulnews/41-everyone-everywhere-is-living-longer/)

**Towards a more nutritious information diet…**

David

title: Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year revealed
subtitle: A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of…
feedText:
The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico. Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year. Leisure and wellness projects win big again

The judges hailed the biophilic project as "beautifully minimalist with a spiritual touch of the soul". "It's totally fresh, totally innovative, and never seen bef…
articleBody:
A tree-top [sauna](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/saunas/) that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.

The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including [Canada](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/canada/), [France](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/france/), [India](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/india/), [Japan](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/japan/) and [Mexico](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/mexico/).

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.

**Leisure and wellness projects win big again**

The judges hailed the [biophilic](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/biophilic-design/) project as "beautifully minimalist with a spiritual touch of the soul".

"It's totally fresh, totally innovative, and never seen before," they added.

The win marks the second consecutive year that the leisure and wellness project of the year has gone on to claim the overall sector title, following [Herzog & de Meuron's win last year](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/11/25/herzog-de-meuron-win-dezeen-awards-2025-architecture-project-of-the-year/).

- ## Architecture project of the year announced Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi

Previous

Next

The winning project of the year was up against category winners including [a sprawling brick-clad university building modelled on stepped wells](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/02/24/sanjay-puri-architects-prestige-university/) in India, [a country house with walls formed of unstabilised rammed earth](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/04/01/rammed-earth-house-video-tuckey-design-studio/) in the UK and [a project featuring an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/14/parque-del-jaguar-colectivo-c733-tulum-mexico-ecological-park/) in Mexico.

A [housing project that appears as if emerging from the natural landscape](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/10/la-querola-andorra-jean-nouvel-ribas-ribas-arquitectos-fire/) and [a viewpoint designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the burial site of a legendary Viking](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/10/ring-bjolfur-arkibygg-architects-esja/) were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning architecture projects below:

Photos by Daichi

**Architecture project of the year and leisure and wellness project** **of the year: Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi**

The project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of [Tokyo](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/tokyo/), and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest [cabins](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/cabins/) and additional sauna spaces.

> Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly

The idea for the project was to make the trees feel part of the architecture, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

"Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly," said the master jury.

"It is a building that offers a spiritual connection between humans and nature."

[Read more about Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/14/daichi-inc-silent-river-tree-sauna/)

Photos by Toshihisa Ishii

**House (urban) project of the year: Amami House by Sakai Architects**

Local studio Sakai Architects won urban house of the year for its off-grid home on Amami Ōshima, an island in the Amami archipelago off [Japan](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/japan/)'s southern coast.

> This house shows how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature

The design was informed by the region's traditional materials and crafts and its development was spurred by the increase in extreme weather conditions on the island.

"This house shows how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature," the master jury said.

"In a time of [climate crisis](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/climate-change/), it offers an excellent solution for autonomy of energy, while smartly reinterpreting the arrangement and materials of a traditional Japanese house."

[Read more about Amami House](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/01/04/amami-house-sakai-architects-japan/)

Photos by Lv Xiaobin

**House (rural) project of the year: Jiang Deng Lu by Shisuo Design Office**

Shisuo Design Office won rural house of the year for Jiang Deng Lu in Anhui, [China](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/China/).

> This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result

The compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site and made using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client's own factory.

"This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result," said the judges.

"Innovative in its use of available materials, the project is highly resolved, with incredible quality of light and generosity of space despite a small footprint."

[Read more about Jiang Deng Lu](https://www.dezeen.com/?p=2385241)

Photos by Pepo Vazquez Cortes

**Housing project of the year: La Querola by Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos**

Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos won housing project of the year for La Querola in Ordino, Andorra.

> A deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core.

Made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley and clad in locally sourced slate, the building's facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor [terraces](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/terrace/).

The judges commended the development's trend-bucking design as a "deliberately expressionist project, celebrating forms that are not repeatable".

"It's a deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core. It's unconventional, unique, controversial, and a very strong statement," they said.

Recently, a fire damaged all seven buildings in the uninhabited development. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

[Read more about La Querola](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/10/la-querola-andorra-jean-nouvel-ribas-ribas-arquitectos-fire/)

Photos by Shinya Sato

**House renovation of the year: Haniyasu House by Aatismo**

Local architecture studio Aatismo won house renovation of the year for Haniyasu House, a home in the coastal town of Kamakura, Japan.

> It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability

The project saw the single-storey home, originally built in 1967, stripped back to its timber frame after a typhoon had left it structurally unsound, and boldly characterised with rough walls streaked with clay, soil and metal powders to evoke ceramic glazes.

The judges praised the project's sensitivity to "the history of both the architecture and its owners".

"It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability,” they added.

[Read more about Haniyasu House](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/03/08/aatismo-haniyasu-house/)

Photos by Parham Taghioff

**House extension of the year: Golmorad by ZAV Architects**

Iranian studio [ZAV Architects](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/zav-architects/) won house extension of the year for its project featuring a series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue in Tehran, [Iran](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/iran/).

> It's clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life.

Transforming the residence from a weekend villa into a permanent home, its arched series of overlapping arched roofs appears as if organically growing from the home.

The judges found the extension to be "playful with a sense of freedom," adding that, "it doesn't manipulate the old house in any way, but instead seems to organically extend it in a very unpredictable direction."

"It's clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life," they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

[Read more about Golmorad](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/10/golmorad-extension-zav-architects/)

Photos by Martin Argyroglo

**Civic project of the year: Zando Central Market by Think Tank Architecture**

French studio Think Tank Architecture won civic project of the year for its geometric brick-and-concrete market in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo.

> A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves

The new building, with space for 20,000 vendors, replaces a historic market on the same site in the capital that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

"A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves, and a capacity to serve the community in a really large-scale way," said the master jury.

"It has a variety within it to allow a lot of activity to take place, with materials that are simple but sustainable."

[Read more about Zando Central Market](https://www.dezeen.com/?p=2384054)

Photos by Farshid Moussavi Architecture

**Cultural project of the year: Ismaili Center Houston by Farshid Moussavi Architecture**

[Farshid Moussavi Architects](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/farshid-moussavi/) won cultural project of the year for its Ismaili Center in [Houston](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/houston/), United States.

> A very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner

The building and its sprawling gardens is the first Ismaili Center in the US and is one of several around the world commissioned by the current Imam, or spiritual leader, of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community to serve as a place of worship and cultural exchange.

The judges praised it as a "very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner".

"It has a stunning relationship to light, and incredible detailing and materiality," they added.

[Read more about Ismaili Center Houston](https://www.dezeen.com/2025/11/07/farshid-moussavi-ismaili-center-houston/)

Photos by DONG Image

**Workplace project (small) of the year:** **Carpenter's Home by Primary Architects**

Chinese studio Primary Architects won small workplace project of the year for its undulating timber roof-topped studio in Xinyang, China.

> The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities

The project, a local carpenter's studio, was designed by the practice to incorporate the craftsman's studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public.

"A beautiful project that goes above and beyond the brief," commended the judges.

"The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities."

[Read more about Carpenter's Home](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/10/primary-architects-carpenters-home-china/)

Photos by Turner Works

**Workplace project (large) of the year: Florentia Village by Turner Works**

Architecture studio [Turner Works](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/turner-works/) won large workplace project of the year for Florentia Village, London.

> Well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour

The practice transformed an old [textile](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/textiles/) manufacturing site in London's Harringay Warehouse District into a creative hub that offers flexible workshops, studios and industrial units ranging from 46 to 1,400 square metres, alongside community spaces and a cafe.

The judges praised it as "well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour," as well as the buildings being "highly flexible, with spaces designed to reinforce a sense of community".

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

[Read more about Florentia Village](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/02/06/florentia-village-turner-works/)

Photos by Vinay Panjwani

**Education project of the year: Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects**

[Sanjay Puri Architects](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/sanjay-puri/) won education project of the year for its sprawling brick-clad university building in Indore, [India](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/india/).

> In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most new constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould

Referencing traditional stepped wells found in the country, its defining feature is its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof, which comprises 463 stepped platforms that can be used as individual social spaces or as a singular auditorium for up to 9,000 people

“This project creates its own universe," said the master jury.

"In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most new constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould," they continued.

"The massing of the roof reduces scale and creates interesting courtyards, creating spaces that feel appropriate for both the place and its climate."

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

[Read more about Prestige University](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/02/24/sanjay-puri-architects-prestige-university/)

Photos by Romain Meffre & Yves Marchand

**Heritage project of the year: Olympics Utilities by Chartier-Corbasson Architects**

French studio [Chartier-Corbasson Architectes](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/chartier-corbasson-architectes/) won heritage project of the year for its transformation of a neglected underground passage beneath [Paris](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/paris/), France.

> It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant

Located in a passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens, the studio created a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a new purpose.

"It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant," said the judges.

"The project creates architectural character, while also preserving a connection to 19th-century futuristic architecture. Unusual, but iconic."

[Read more about Olympics Utilities](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/11/public-toilets-chartier-corbasson-paris/)

Photos by Giorgos Sfakianakis

**Hospitality project of the year: Perma by Mold Architects**

Perma by [Mold Architects](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/mold-architects/) in Serifos, [Greece](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/greece/) won hospitality project of the year,

> There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint

Comprising five guest houses, the rugged retreat on the island of Serifos was constructed by using material extracted during construction to build much of the retreat itself, rather than removing the hillside and building on top of it.

The judges praised its "striking architecture", noting it as "very innovative in its programmatic possibilities".

"There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint," they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

[Read more about Perma](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/07/01/perma-guest-retreat-mold-architects-serifos-island-aegean-sea/)

Photos by Roland Halbe

**Infrastructure and transport project of the year: Naples Underground Central Station by Miralles Tagliabue EMBT**

Spanish architecture studio [EMBT](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/embt/) won infrastructure and transport project of the year for Naples Underground Central Station in [Italy](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/italy/).

> A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train

Contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof, the 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a new public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city.

The judges commended the project as a "successful urban space, both elegant and spatially interesting."

"A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train," they continued. "The use of timber is also impressive."

[Read more about Naples Underground Central Station](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/12/embt-naples-underground-central-station/)

Photos by Studio CAPN

**Small project of the year: Ring of Bjólfur** **by Arkibygg Architects**

Local studios [Arkibygg Architects](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/arkibygg-arkitektar/) and [Esja Architecture](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/esja-architecture/) won small project of the year for their mountain viewpoint in Seyðisfjörður, Iceland.

> A minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way

Designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

The master jury hailed the viewpoint as a "minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way," adding that, "the minimal use of material maximises the experience".

[Read more about Ring of Bjólfur](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/10/ring-bjolfur-arkibygg-architects-esja/)

Photos by David Valinsky

**Mixed-use project of the year: York Minster Centre of Excellence by Tonkin Liu**

Architecture studio [Tonkin Liu](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/tonkin-liu/)won mixed-use project of the year for its two timber buildings on either side of a Grade I-listed Gothic cathedral in [York](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/york/), United Kingdom.

> The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a new generation of makers using the space

Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stonemasons views of the historic York Minster cathedral.

"There is a real honesty in the combination of buildings, with a unique roofing structure," said the judges.

"The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a new generation of makers using the space," they added.

[Read more about York Minster Centre of Excellence](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/11/york-minster-centre-excellence-tonkin-liu/)

Photos by Rafael Gamo

**Landscape and urban design of the year: Parque del Jaguar by Colectivo C733**

Mexican studio [Colectivo C733](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/colectivo-c733/) won landscape and urban design of the year for its work across Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.

> Despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects

The project aims to safeguard one of the region's important habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

It features an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows [wildlife](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/animals/) to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest, as well as a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals' habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The judges praised the project as "rooted in its context, made for locals as well as tourists," adding that, "despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects."

[Read more about Parque del Jaguar](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/14/parque-del-jaguar-colectivo-c733-tulum-mexico-ecological-park/)

Photos by Fran Mart

**Sustainable building of the year: Rammed Earth House by Tuckey Design Studio**

Rammed Earth house by [Tuckey Design Studio](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/tuckey-design-studio/) in Wiltshire, United Kingdom, won sustainable building of the year,

> Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe

Built on the site of a former brickworks, the rural country house was constructed from both the clay underfoot and an aggregate made from crushed demolition waste to form unstabilised rammed earth walls.

As a form of earth construction that is largely untested at such scale in the UK, the judges commended the project as "a radical example of material innovation".

"Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe," they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

[Read more about Rammed Earth House](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/04/01/rammed-earth-house-video-tuckey-design-studio/)

Photos by De Nederlandsche Bank Ossip Architectuurfotografie

**Sustainable renovation of the year: De Nederlandsche Bank by Mecanoo**

Dutch firm [Mecanoo](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/Mecanoo/) won sustainable renovation of the year for its major renovation of the Netherlands' central bank in [Amsterdam](https://www.dezeen.com/tag/amsterdam/).

> An admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building

The project involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault, seeing a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation's ugliest building.

The renovation was praised as "an admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building," by the master jury, who also noted its efforts to adapt it to a different use "while also addressing material and energy concerns."

[Read more about De Nederlandsche Bank](https://www.dezeen.com/2026/11/15/netherlands-central-bank-renovation-mecanoo/)

**Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with Trimble**
Dezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company [Trimble](https://www.trimble.com/blog/trimble/en-US/article/trimble-sponsors-dezeen-awards?utm_source=trimble-website&utm_medium=article). articleBody:
### “Creative fantasy, because it is mainly trying to do something else … may open your hoard and let all the locked things fly away like cage-birds.”

*“I do not believe that I have ever written a children’s book,”* the great [Maurice Sendak](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/maurice-sendak/) once said [in an interview](https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/12/29/tateshorts-maurice-sendak/). *“I don’t write for children,”* he [told Colbert](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/05/09/grim-colberty-tales-maurice-sendak/). *“I write — and somebody says, ‘That’s for children!’”* This sentiment — the idea that designating certain types of literature as “children’s” is a choice entirely arbitrary and entirely made by adults — has since been [eloquently echoed by Neil Gaiman](http://explore.noodle.org/post/64133968491/i-dont-think-there-is-such-a-thing-as-a-bad-book), but isn’t, in fact, a new idea.

On March 8, 1939, **J.R.R. Tolkien** (January 3, 1892–September 2, 1973), celebrated as one of the greatest fantasy writers in history, gave a lecture titled “Fairy Stories,” eventually adapted into an essay retitled “On Fairy-Stories” and included in the appendix to [Tales from the Perilous Realm](http://www.amazon.com/Tales-Perilous-Realm-J-R-R-Tolkien/dp/0547154119/?tag=braipick-20) ([public library](http://www.worldcat.org/title/tales-from-the-perilous-realm/oclc/243480382&referer=brief_results)). At the crux of his argument, which explores the nature of fantasy and the cultural role of fairy tales, is the same profound conviction that there is no such thing as writing “for children.”

One of Tolkien’s a href=”https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/11/01/art-of-the-hobbit/”>original illustrations for the first edition of *The Hobbit*, 1936

Tolkien begins at the beginning, by defining what a fairy tale is:

> A “fairy-story” is one which touches on or uses Faerie, whatever its own main purpose may be: satire, adventure, morality, fantasy. Faerie itself may perhaps most nearly be translated by Magic — but it is magic of a peculiar mood and power, at the furthest pole from the vulgar devices of the laborious, scientific, magician. There is one proviso: if there is any satire present in the tale, one thing must not be made fun of, the magic itself. That must in that story be taken seriously, neither laughed at nor explained away.

Illustration for Hans Christian Andersen’s ‘The Snow Queen’ by Katharine Beverley and Elizabeth Ellender, 1929. Click image for details.

He then explores the relationship between fairy tales and language, denouncing Max Müller’s view of mythology as a “disease of language”:

> Mythology is not a disease at all, though it may like all human things become diseased. You might as well say that thinking is a disease of the mind. It would be more near the truth to say that languages, especially modern European languages, are a disease of mythology. But Language cannot, all the same, be dismissed. The incarnate mind, the tongue, and the tale are in our world coeval. The human mind, endowed with the powers of generalization and abstraction, sees not only green-grass, discriminating it from other things (and finding it fair to look upon), but sees that it is green as well as being grass. But how powerful, how stimulating to the very faculty that produced it, was the invention of the adjective: no spell or incantation in Faerie is more potent. And that is not surprising: such incantations might indeed be said to be only another view of adjectives, a part of speech in a mythical grammar. The mind that thought of light, heavy, grey, yellow, still, swift, also conceived of magic that would make heavy things light and able to fly, turn grey lead into yellow gold, and the still rock into a swift water. If it could do the one, it could do the other; it inevitably did both. When we can take green from grass, blue from heaven, and red from blood, we have already an enchanter’s power — upon one plane; and the desire to wield that power in the world external to our minds awakes. It does not follow that we shall use that power well upon any plane. We may put a deadly green upon a man’s face and produce a horror; we may make the rare and terrible blue moon to shine; or we may cause woods to spring with silver leaves and rams to wear fleeces of gold, and put hot fire into the belly of the cold worm. But in such “fantasy,” as it is called, new form is made; Faerie begins; Man becomes a sub-creator.

Illustration for Hans Christian Andersen’s ‘The Darning Needle’ by Maurice Sendak, 1959. Click image for details.

Like Sendak and Gaiman, Tolkien insists that fairy tales aren’t inherently “for” children but that we, as adults, simply decide that they are, based on a series of misconceptions about both the nature of this literature and the nature of children:

> It is usually assumed that children are the natural or the specially appropriate audience for fairy-stories. In describing a fairy-story which they think adults might possibly read for their own entertainment, reviewers frequently indulge in such waggeries as: “this book is for children from the ages of six to sixty.” But I have never yet seen the puff of a new motor-model that began thus: “this toy will amuse infants from seventeen to seventy”; though that to my mind would be much more appropriate. Is there any essential connexion between children and fairy-stories? Is there any call for comment, if an adult reads them for himself? Reads them as tales, that is, not studies them as curios. Adults are allowed to collect and study anything, even old theatre programmes or paper bags.
> […]
> Among those who still have enough wisdom not to think fairy-stories pernicious, the common opinion seems to be that there is a natural connexion between the minds of children and fairy-stories, of the same order as the connexion between children’s bodies and milk. I think this is an error; at best an error of false sentiment, and one that is therefore most often made by those who, for whatever private reason (such as childlessness), tend to think of children as a special kind of creature, almost a different race, rather than as normal, if immature, members of a particular family, and of the human family at large.

Illustration for Howard Pyle’s ‘The Swan Maiden’ by Alice and Martin Provensen, 1971. Click image for details.

He argues, instead, that the stereotype of fairy tales being associated with children and native to their world is “an accident of our domestic history”:

> Fairy-stories have in the modern lettered world been relegated to the “nursery,” as shabby or old-fashioned furniture is relegated to the play-room, primarily because the adults do not want it, and do not mind if it is misused. It is not the choice of the children which decides this. Children as a class—except in a common lack of experience they are not one—neither like fairy-stories more, nor understand them better than adults do; and no more than they like many other things. They are young and growing, and normally have keen appetites, so the fairy-stories as a rule go down well enough. But in fact only some children, and some adults, have any special taste for them; and when they have it, it is not exclusive, nor even necessarily dominant. It is a taste, too, that would not appear, I think, very early in childhood without artificial stimulus; it is certainly one that does not decrease but increases with age, if it is innate.
> […]
> The nursery and schoolroom are merely given such tastes and glimpses of the adult thing as seem fit for them in adult opinion (often much mistaken). Any one of these things would, if left altogether in the nursery, become gravely impaired. So would a beautiful table, a good picture, or a useful machine (such as a microscope), be defaced or broken, if it were left long unregarded in a schoolroom. Fairy-stories banished in this way, cut off from a full adult art, would in the end be ruined; indeed in so far as they have been so banished, they have been ruined.

Tolkien then moves on to the subject of fantasy, a frequently misunderstood faculty of the imagination.

> The mental power of image-making is one thing, or aspect; and it should appropriately be called Imagination. The perception of the image, the grasp of its implications, and the control, which are necessary to a successful expression, may vary in vividness and strength: but this is a difference of degree in Imagination, not a difference in kind. The achievement of the expression, which gives (or seems to give) “the inner consistency of reality,” is indeed another thing, or aspect, needing another name: Art, the operative link between Imagination and the final result, Sub-creation. For my present purpose I require a word which shall embrace both the Sub- creative Art in itself and a quality of strangeness and wonder in the Expression, derived from the Image: a quality essential to fairy-story. I propose, therefore, to arrogate to myself the powers of Humpty-Dumpty, and to use Fantasy for this purpose: in a sense, that is, which combines with its older and higher use as an equivalent of Imagination the derived notions of “unreality” (that is, of unlikeness to the Primary World), of freedom from the domination of observed “fact,” in short of the fantastic. I am thus not only aware but glad of the etymological and semantic connexions of fantasy with fantastic: with images of things that are not only “not actually present,” but which are indeed not to be found in our primary world at all, or are generally believed not to be found there. But while admitting that, I do not assent to the depreciative tone. That the images are of things not in the primary world (if that indeed is possible) is a virtue, not a vice. Fantasy (in this sense) is, I think, not a lower but a higher form of Art, indeed the most nearly pure form, and so (when achieved) the most potent.

Illustration for the fairy tales of Hans Christian Andersen by Japanese artist Takeo Takei, 1928. Click image for details.

He goes on to argue that, despite the many misconceptions that envelop it, fantasy is far more challenging an art than nonfiction, for it necessitates the creation of an elaborate, immersive world from scratch, without the crutch of reality:

> Fantasy … is difficult to achieve. Fantasy may be, as I think, not less but more sub-creative; but at any rate it is found in practice that “the inner consistency of reality” is more difficult to produce, the more unlike are the images and the rearrangements of primary material to the actual arrangements of the Primary World. It is easier to produce this kind of “reality” with more “sober” material. Fantasy thus, too often, remains undeveloped; it is and has been used frivolously, or only half-seriously, or merely for decoration: it remains merely “fanciful.” Anyone inheriting the fantastic device of human language can say the green sun. Many can then imagine or picture it. But that is not enough — though it may already be a more potent thing than many a “thumbnail sketch” or “transcript of life” that receives literary praise.
> To make a Secondary World inside which the green sun will be credible, commanding Secondary Belief, will probably require labour and thought, and will certainly demand a special skill, a kind of elvish craft. Few attempt such difficult tasks. But when they are attempted and in any degree accomplished then we have a rare achievement of Art: indeed narrative art, story-making in its primary and most potent mode.

Scandinavian fairy tale illustration by Kay Nielsen, 1914. Click image for details.

Tolkien makes a curious argument about the oil-and-water relationship between fantasy and drama, managing to slip in a subtle dig at none other than The Bard:

> In human art Fantasy is a thing best left to words, to true literature. … It is a misfortune that Drama, an art fundamentally distinct from Literature, should so commonly be considered together with it, or as a branch of it. Among these misfortunes we may reckon the depreciation of Fantasy. For in part at least this depreciation is due to the natural desire of critics to cry up the forms of literature or “imagination” that they themselves, innately or by training, prefer. And criticism in a country that has produced so great a Drama, and possesses the works of William Shakespeare, tends to be far too dramatic. But Drama is naturally hostile to Fantasy. Fantasy, even of the simplest kind, hardly ever succeeds in Drama, when that is presented as it should be, visibly and audibly acted. Fantastic forms are not to be counterfeited. Men dressed up as talking animals may achieve buffoonery or mimicry, but they do not achieve Fantasy....
> In Macbeth, when it is read, I find the witches tolerable: they have a narrative function and some hint of dark significance; though they are vulgarized, poor things of their kind. They are almost intolerable in the play. They would be quite intolerable, if I were not fortified by some memory of them as they are in the story as read. I am told that I should feel differently if I had the mind of the period, with its witch-hunts and witch-trials. But that is to say: if I regarded the witches as possible, indeed likely, in the Primary World; in other words, if they ceased to be “Fantasy.” That argument concedes the point. To be dissolved, or to be degraded, is the likely fate of Fantasy when a dramatist tries to use it, even such a dramatist as Shakespeare. Macbeth is indeed a work by a playwright who ought, at least on this occasion, to have written a story, if he had the skill or patience for that art.

Illustration for The Fairy Tales of E. E. Cummings by John Eaton, 1965. Click image for details.

Another misconception Tolkien debunks — speaking to Susan Sontag’s conviction that [polarities only rob life of dimension](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/12/03/susan-sontag-stereotypes-polarities/) — is the notion that the fantastical is somehow diametrically opposed to the rational:

> Fantasy is a natural human activity. It certainly does not destroy or even insult Reason; and it does not either blunt the appetite for, nor obscure the perception of, scientific verity. On the contrary. The keener and the clearer is the reason, the better fantasy will it make. If men were ever in a state in which they did not want to know or could not perceive truth (facts or evidence), then Fantasy would languish until they were cured. If they ever get into that state (it would not seem at all impossible), Fantasy will perish, and become Morbid Delusion.
> For creative Fantasy is founded upon the hard recognition that things are so in the world as it appears under the sun; on a recognition of fact, but not a slavery to it. So upon logic was founded the nonsense that displays itself in the tales and rhymes of Lewis Carroll. If men really could not distinguish between frogs and men, fairy-stories about frog-kings would not have arisen.

Returning to his notion of the Secondary World driven by Secondary Belief, Tolkien contributes to [history’s greatest definitions of art](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/06/22/what-is-art/):

> Art is the human process that produces by the way (it is not its only or ultimate object) Secondary Belief.

Illustration for Seamus MacManus’s ‘Feather O’ My Wing’ by Alice and Martin Provensen, 1971. Click image for details.

He then adds to [the psychological functions of art](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/10/25/art-as-therapy-alain-de-botton-john-armstrong/) by exploring the psychological functions of fairy tales, chief among which is their capacity for rebooting our [chronically blunted attention](https://www.themarginalian.org/2013/10/25/art-as-therapy-alain-de-botton-john-armstrong/):

> Recovery (which includes return and renewal of health) is a re-gaining—regaining of a clear view. I do not say “seeing things as they are” and involve myself with the philosophers, though I might venture to say “seeing things as we are (or were) meant to see them”—as things apart from ourselves. We need, in any case, to clean our windows; so that the things seen clearly may be freed from the drab blur of triteness or familiarity—from possessiveness. Of all faces those of our familiares are the ones both most difficult to play fantastic tricks with, and most difficult really to see with fresh attention, perceiving their likeness and unlikeness: that they are faces, and yet unique faces. This triteness is really the penalty of “appropriation”: the things that are trite, or (in a bad sense) familiar, are the things that we have appropriated, legally or mentally. We say we know them. They have become like the things which once attracted us by their glitter, or their colour, or their shape, and we laid hands on them, and then locked them in our hoard, acquired them, and acquiring ceased to look at them.
> […]
> Creative fantasy, because it is mainly trying to do something else (make something new), may open your hoard and let all the locked things fly away like cage-birds.

Illustration for The Fairy Tales of E. E. Cummings by John Eaton, 1965. Click image for details.

The full fifteen-page essay, as well as the rest of [Tales from the Perilous Realm](http://www.amazon.com/Tales-Perilous-Realm-J-R-R-Tolkien/dp/0547154119/?tag=braipick-20), is well worth a read. Complement it with [Tolkien’s little-known illustrations](https://www.themarginalian.org/2011/11/01/art-of-the-hobbit/) for the first edition of *The Hobbit*.

### donating = loving

For seventeen years, I have been spending hundreds of hours and thousands of dollars each month composing *The Marginalian* (which [bore the outgrown name Brain Pickings](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/10/22/brain-pickings-becoming-the-marginalian/) for its first fifteen years). It has remained free and ad-free and alive thanks to patronage from readers. I have no staff, no interns, no assistant — a thoroughly one-woman labor of love that is also my life and my livelihood. If this labor makes your own life more livable in any way, please consider lending a helping hand with a [donation](https://www.themarginalian.org/donate/). Your support makes all the difference.

### newsletter

*The Marginalian* has a free weekly newsletter. It comes out on Sundays and offers the week’s most inspiring reading. Here’s [what to expect](https://mailchi.mp/brainpickings/janna-levin-rebecca-elson-anne-lamott-james-gleick). Like? [Sign up.](https://www.themarginalian.org/newsletter/)

articleBody:
Please consider [giving a donation to FactCheck.org](https://giving.aws.cloud.upenn.edu/fund?fastStart=simpleForm&program=ANS&fund=602014) during our annual end-of-year fundraising drive, which starts today and lasts until the end of the year.

We’re setting a goal of $75,000 in contributions to help fund our work in 2027, as the Democrats take control of Congress and presidential contenders start vying for attention.

Competing claims from President Donald Trump and a Democratic Congress, as well as open presidential primaries for both parties, will surely keep us busy.

Not that we weren’t already.

If you read our midterms coverage of toss-up Senate races and campaign talking points, please consider a donation.

If you appreciate that we keep tabs on the claims the president and leaders in Congress make, sorting fact from fiction, please consider a donation.

If you’re a fan of our SciCheck project, which debunks falsehoods and explains what we know about scientific topics, such as vaccination and climate change, please consider a donation.

We’re a nonprofit project of the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. We don’t keep our content behind any paywalls, and we don’t accept advertising. We avoid even the appearance of a conflict of interest by not accepting contributions from unions, partisan organizations or political advocacy groups.

Our funding overwhelmingly comes from an APPC endowment, which includes funding from the Annenberg Foundation and the Annenberg School for Communication Trust at the University of Pennsylvania. But individual donations have helped to keep us operating, 23 years after we first started holding politicians accountable for the claims they make. Thank you for your support.

If you’d like to make a gift, credit card donations may be made through [our “Donate” page](https://giving.aws.cloud.upenn.edu/fund?fastStart=simpleForm&program=ANS&fund=602014).

If you prefer to give by check, send to: FactCheck.org, Annenberg Public Policy Center, P.O. Box 58100, Philadelphia, PA 19102. Checks can be made payable to “The Trustees of the University of Pennsylvania” with a note in the memo field indicating the donation is for FactCheck.org.

The University of Pennsylvania is a 501(c)(3) organization, and your contribution is deductible from U.S. federal income taxes to the full extent allowed by law.

Our policy is to disclose the identity of anyone who contributes $5,000 or more in a given year. Most of the contributions we receive are much smaller — $25 or less. You can read our annual and quarterly [financial reports](https://factcheck.us5.list-manage.com/track/click?u=17a60fa3d47b33b686b744ff5&id=e457de04e7&e=6f09f3a9d3) on our website.

We greatly appreciate your support.

title: EU plant Digital Fairness Act: Probeabos sollen nicht mehr still verlängern

articleBody:
**Ein Gratismonat ist schnell gebucht und noch schneller vergessen, bis die erste Abbuchung kommt. Dieses Muster will Brüssel durchbrechen. Vergangenen Mittwoch hat die EU-Kommission den Entwurf für den Digital Fairness Act präsentiert, ein Verbraucherschutzgesetz für Onlineshops, Abodienste, soziale Netzwerke und Mobile Games.**

Die EU-Kommission [nimmt](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/legislative-train/theme-protecting-our-democracy-upholding-our-values/file-digital-fairness-act) damit Abofallen, Fake-Rabatte und manipulative App-Designs ins Visier. Bis daraus ein Gesetz wird, dauert es aber wohl noch. Kern des Vorhabens ist eine Liste mit 62 Geschäftspraktiken, die in der EU pauschal untersagt werden sollen. Zehn Einträge widmen sich den sogenannten Dark Patterns, mit denen Apps und Webseiten ihre Besucher in eine bestimmte Richtung schieben. Darunter fallen vorgetäuschte Lagerknappheit, bereits angehakte Zusatzkäufe und Pop-ups, die sich immer wieder aufdrängen. Ebenso tabu wären erfundene Preisnachlässe und Buchungen, die am Ende teurer sind als zu Beginn angezeigt.

## Vor allem Freemium-Apps im Fokus

Am deutlichsten dürftet ihr die neuen Regeln bei Abos spüren. Eine Testphase mündet laut Entwurf nur dann in einen kostenpflichtigen Vertrag, wenn ihr vorher erinnert wurdet und ausdrücklich zustimmt. Vor jeder automatischen Verlängerung ist ein Hinweis fällig, kündigen soll mit wenigen Klicks möglich sein, und auf Wunsch muss ein Mensch erreichbar sein. Dass das Thema auch Apple betrifft, zeigten zuletzt Berichte aus den USA: Dort sollen Store-Mitarbeiter Probeabos gebucht haben, ohne dass Kunden selbst zustimmten.

## Influencer sollen ebenfalls unter Beobachtung gestellt werden

Auch Influencer nimmt der Entwurf in die Pflicht. Werbung muss klar erkennbar sein, für Versäumnisse haften die Auftraggeber mit. Spieler unter 18 Jahren sollen weder kostenpflichtige Lootboxen kaufen noch auf Pay-to-win-Modelle treffen.

## Doomscrooling wird überraschend moderat behandelt

Weniger streng geht die Kommission mit Funktionen um, die zum Dranbleiben verleiten. Infinite Scrolling, automatisch startende Videos und Streaks werden nicht verboten, Anbieter müssen aber einen Ausschalter anbieten. Gleiches ist für KI-Begleiter vorgesehen, die Nähe vortäuschen. Aus dem EU-Parlament und von Bürgerrechtlern kommt dazu der Einwand, die Verantwortung liege damit weiter bei den Nutzern.

## Strafenkatalog ebenfalls schon skizziert

In besonders großen, länderübergreifenden Fällen will die Kommission künftig selbst einschreiten. Das Strafmaß reicht dann bis zu sechs Prozent des globalen Jahresumsatzes. Nach eigener Rechnung der Behörde bleiben Verbrauchern durch das Paket jährlich bis zu 13,7 Milliarden Euro mehr in der Tasche. Noch ist nichts davon in Kraft. Zunächst verhandeln Parlament und Mitgliedstaaten über den Text, ein Startdatum steht nicht fest. Erfahrungsgemäß ziehen sich solche Verfahren über Jahre, und Details können sich dabei noch verschieben. In Deutschland bleibt es vorerst beim Kündigungsbutton und beim Widerrufsbutton, der seit Juni Pflicht ist.

articleBody:
Looming over the quiet countryside of An Nhon, Hoang De Citadel represents an extraordinary historical palimpsest where two distinct Vietnamese empires converged upon a single plot of land.

Originally built in the eleventh century as Vijaya, the formidable stone-walled capital of the Champa Kingdom, the grounds were transformed in 1776 when Emperor Nguyen Nhac established it as the imperial stronghold of the Tay Son movement.

Beneath its current overgrown earthen ramparts lie layers of complex history: medieval Cham elephant sculptures and carved stone guardians stand alongside ruined Tay Son palace foundations and later Nguyen Dynasty tombs.

Walking through its weathered stone gates reveals an unsettling, atmospheric blend of ancient spiritual art and military strategy, offering a profound glimpse into a fortress that witnessed the rise and fall of rival dynasties.

title: Mit Hubertus Heil wird sich die SPD nicht neu erfinden
subtitle: Was soll Hubertus Heil auch sonst tun, als sich auf den Parteivorsitz der SPD zu bewerben?
feedText: Schließlich sitzt er schon seit 1998 im Bundestag und war bereits Generalsekretär sowie Minister. Weniger sinnvoll erscheint die Kandidatur jedoch unter dem Gesichtspunkt der Erneuerung, der praktisch alle in der SPD das Wort reden. Auch Heil selbst kommt natürlich nicht darum herum, seiner Partei Aufbruch zu versprechen. Nur kann er diesen nicht glaubhaft vertreten, nachdem er über Jahrzehnte bei allem dabei gewesen ist, was in der SPD schief läuft.

Nur kann er diesen nicht glaubhaft vertreten, nachdem er über Jahrzehnte bei allem dabei gewesen ist, was in der SPD schief läuft.

title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
subtitle: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach.
